passages.title: Draw me after you

verses.t: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine.
Your oils are sweet to breathe; your name is oil poured out. No wonder the young women love you.
Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his rooms. We will rejoice and be glad in you; we will praise your love more than wine. How right they are to love you!

passages.essence: The Song opens with no story and no introduction, only a woman’s voice already in the middle of longing. She asks for a kiss, praises his love above wine, and pulls him, and us, into the room.
reading: After a one-line title, the first voice we hear is a woman’s, and the first thing she wants is a kiss. There is no narrator, no setting, no names. This is typical of the whole Song: it does not tell a story so much as let us overhear lovers speaking, and it begins, as desire does, in the middle. The opening line is literally “let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth”, a doubling that is not redundant but insistent: real kisses, mouth to mouth, not a formal greeting.

Then the pronoun jumps: “let him kiss me… for your love is better than wine.” She speaks about him and to him in the same breath. Readers used to tidy grammar have tried to fix this, but the shift is common in Hebrew poetry and true to experience: the absent lover is talked about and talked to at once, as if he were half in the room. The same restless movement between “he”, “you” and “we” runs through verse 4.

Verse 3 is built on a pun. “Oil” is šemen and “name” is šēm: your oils smell sweet, your name is oil poured out. His reputation travels the way perfume fills a house when a flask is opened; to say his name is already to breathe him in. Scent will be one of the Song’s main languages. Wine, oil, nard, myrrh: the lovers are known through taste and smell before they are described by sight.

In verse 4 the scene tightens. “Draw me after you; let us run” is a plea and an invitation at once. “The king has brought me into his rooms” introduces the royal language that will come and go through the poem. Most modern scholars think the “king” here is not a literal monarch but a lover’s title, as a bride and groom were called king and queen in later wedding custom; to her he is royalty. The “we” who rejoice may be the young women of verse 3, a chorus that will reappear as the daughters of Jerusalem.

The passage ends where it began, with love better than wine, and with a small, generous line: “How right they are to love you!” Her desire is not jealous or secretive. She is glad that others see what she sees. The opening sets the Song’s key: frank, joyful, sensory, and spoken by a woman who is not waiting to be chosen but asks.

words.note: A Hebrew superlative, like “holy of holies” or “king of kings”: the finest song, the song above all songs. The title’s phrase “which is Solomon’s” (’ăšer lišlōmōh) can mean by, for, about or in the style of Solomon. The Hebrew of the Song has late features and at least one Persian loanword, so most scholars date it well after Solomon; the name attaches it to Israel’s great patron of wisdom and love poetry.

Plural of dôd, which elsewhere means “beloved” or “uncle”. In the plural it means physical love: in Proverbs 7:18 the seductress says “let us drink our fill of dōdîm till morning”. The translation keeps the gentler “love” because the Song uses the word for the whole experience of loving, but the bodily sense is primary. The same root gives dôdî, “my beloved”, the woman’s name for him throughout.

From māšaḵ, to pull or draw out, as one draws a bow or a rope. Jeremiah 31:3 uses it of God: “with faithful love I have drawn you”. That echo made this line central for allegorical readers, who heard the soul asking to be pulled toward God. In the plain sense it is simply a woman taking her lover’s hand and saying: take me with you.

The pun of verse 3. Your name is “oil poured out”, where the verb form (tûraq) is unusual and may hide a rare word for a kind of perfume, but the sense is clear. A name in Hebrew is not a label but a presence and a reputation. Ecclesiastes 7:1 makes the same pairing: “a good name is better than good oil.”

history: Rabbi Akiva, defending the Song’s place in scripture at the council of Yavneh, said that all the writings are holy but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5). The Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase, reads these opening verses as Israel at Sinai: the “kisses of his mouth” are the words of the Torah given face to face, and the oils and name are the fame of God’s deeds at the Exodus. Rashi follows this line, hearing a people in exile remembering the first love of the wilderness.

Christian readers took the same lines as the soul or the Church longing for Christ. Origen, whose third-century commentary shaped all later reading, said the bride asks no longer for kisses through intermediaries, the prophets, but from the Bridegroom’s own mouth. Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons on the Song in the twelfth century and only reached the third chapter; the first several are on this kiss alone, which he called the touch of the Word on the soul. Modern scholars read the verses first as human love poetry, and many note parallels with Egyptian love songs of the New Kingdom, where lovers also call each other “brother” and “sister”, speak of perfume and wine, and talk in fragments rather than plots.

life.love: She asks plainly for what she wants. A lot of love goes hungry because no one says “kiss me”, “come closer”, “take me with you”. Notice too her lack of jealousy: she is glad others admire the one she loves. Love that needs the other to be invisible to everyone else is often fear. Try naming, out loud, one thing about someone you love that you are glad the world sees.
life.body: The Song begins with the mouth, with wine, with scent. Before anything is looked at, it is tasted and breathed. We often live in our eyes and our thoughts. Today, let one meal, one drink, one smell be received slowly enough that you actually notice it. Desire is partly attention, and the senses are where attention starts.
life.inner: “Draw me after you; let us run.” Whether you hear this as human love or as longing for God, it admits something honest: we do not always move on our own. Sometimes the first step is asking to be drawn, by a person, a calling, a practice, a source larger than yourself. What would you ask to be drawn toward, if you dared?

passages.question: What do I long for that I have never asked for out loud?

passages.title: Dark and lovely

verses.t: I am dark, and I am lovely, daughters of Jerusalem: dark as the tents of Kedar, lovely as the curtains of Solomon.
Do not stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has gazed on me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards. My own vineyard I have not kept.
Tell me, you whom my soul loves: where do you pasture your flock? Where do you let it rest at noon? Why should I be like a veiled woman, wandering among the flocks of your companions?
If you do not know, most beautiful of women, follow the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.

passages.essence: The woman answers the stares of the city women: she is sunburnt from working her brothers’ vineyards, and lovely all the same. Then she asks her lover where he rests at noon, and he teases her to follow the tracks of the flock.
reading: “I am dark, and I am lovely.” The Hebrew conjunction is the simple wə, which can mean “and” or “but”. Older translations chose “but”, as if beauty had to be granted in spite of darkness. The context supports “and”: she pairs two images of equal value, the black goat-hair tents of Kedar, an Arabian tribe, and the fine curtains of Solomon. Both are dark cloth; both are beautiful. She is not apologising. She is correcting a gaze.

Verse 6 explains the darkness, and it is not ethnic but a matter of work and weather: “the sun has gazed on me.” Fair skin was a mark of a woman who stayed indoors; a tan meant fieldwork. Her “mother’s sons”, a slightly cool way of naming her brothers, were angry with her and put her to work in the vineyards. Then comes one of the Song’s double meanings: “my own vineyard I have not kept.” The vineyard is both literal land and, throughout the Song, her own body and sexuality (8:12 makes this explicit). She has tended other people’s property and neglected herself; she has also, perhaps, not guarded herself as her brothers wished. Both senses are in play.

In verse 7 she turns from the women to her lover. “You whom my soul loves” is her phrase for him, and it will return four times in the night search of chapter 3. She asks where he pastures his flock at noon, the hour of rest in the heat, because she wants to find him without “wandering among the flocks of your companions” like a veiled woman. The veil here may suggest a woman who is a stranger, a mourner, or someone mistaken for a prostitute (as Tamar veiled herself in Genesis 38). She wants to come to him openly.

Verse 8 answers, probably in his voice, with a light teasing tone: if you don’t know, you who are the most beautiful of women, follow the tracks and pasture your kids by the shepherds’ tents. In other words: you can find me, come and see. The pastoral world of shepherds, flocks and noon shade sits beside the royal world of verse 4. The Song moves easily between costumes; lovers are kings and shepherds, queens and vineyard girls, all at once.

words.note: Šəḥôrâ means black or very dark; in verse 6 she uses a diminutive-like form, šəḥarḥōret, “darkish”, “tanned”. Nā’wâ is a word for fitting, seemly beauty. The translation’s “and” follows most modern scholars. The line has a long and painful reception history in debates about skin colour; in the poem itself, she claims her darkness and her beauty together.

The vineyard is one of the Song’s master images. It appears literally (the brothers’ vineyards, the vines in blossom of 2:13) and figuratively for the woman herself: “my own vineyard” here and in 8:12, where she declares it hers to give. Grapes and wine also signify intoxicating love. When the Song says vineyard, ask both what grows there and whom it belongs to.

Nep̄eš is not a ghostly soul but the living self: throat, breath, appetite, life. To love with the nep̄eš is to love with your whole hungry being, as in “love the Lord… with all your nep̄eš” (Deuteronomy 6:5). This is her name for him when he is absent or sought. Note too the short relative particle še-, a feature of later Hebrew that helps date the Song.

history: The Targum and Midrash Song of Songs Rabbah read “dark and lovely” as Israel speaking of herself: dark through the sin of the golden calf, lovely through receiving the Torah; dark in her deeds, lovely in the deeds of her ancestors. Origen read the bride as the Church gathered from the gentiles, dark because she was not from Israel, lovely because she was washed and made beautiful. Some patristic writers saw the Queen of Sheba or the Ethiopian wife of Moses (Numbers 12) behind her.

The phrase has had a heavy afterlife. The Latin Vulgate’s nigra sum sed formosa, “I am black but beautiful”, shaped centuries of art and preaching and was used both to dignify and to demean dark skin. The black Madonnas of medieval Europe were sometimes explained with this verse. In the twentieth century, African American and womanist readers reclaimed the line, and many translations moved from “but” to “and”. Most modern commentators, Roland Murphy and J. Cheryl Exum among them, note that the poem itself explains the darkness as sunburn from labour, and reads her speech as a confident reply to an unkind gaze.

life.love: Family can put us to work on everyone’s vineyard but our own. Her brothers’ anger and demands left her own life untended. Is there a relationship where you have been the dependable worker so long that no one, including you, asks what you need? Love that lasts includes someone who asks, as she does, “where can I find you?”, and means it.
life.body: She is looked at and judged, and she answers without shame: dark and lovely, both. Most of us carry a body that others have commented on. Try her sentence in your own words: “I am this, and I am lovely.” Not in spite of it. The marks of work, sun and time can be part of beauty rather than a subtraction from it.
life.inner: “My own vineyard I have not kept.” Every life has a plot of ground that is ours alone: a gift, a calling, a part of the self. Duties crowd it out. It is not selfish to tend it; it may be the most honest service you can give. What small piece of your own vineyard could you give an hour to this week?

passages.question: Whose vineyard have I been keeping, and what has happened to my own?

passages.title: Nard, myrrh and henna

verses.t: To a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots I compare you, my love.
Your cheeks are lovely between the ornaments, your neck with its strings of beads.
We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
While the king was on his couch, my nard gave out its fragrance.
My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies all night between my breasts.
My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.

passages.essence: For the first time he speaks his praise, comparing her to a mare among Pharaoh’s stallions. She answers with scent: her nard filling the room, and her beloved as a sachet of myrrh resting between her breasts.
reading: His first words of praise can startle a modern ear: “To a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots I compare you.” The image is not about looks but about effect. Egyptian chariots were drawn by stallions; scholars since Marvin Pope have pointed to an ancient tactic of releasing a mare among enemy chariot horses to throw them into chaos. Whether or not the poet knew that story, the sense is clear: she is a magnificent, decorated, disruptive presence among men. The word for “my love” here, ra‘yātî, appears for the first time; it will become his favourite name for her.

Verses 10 and 11 move from the horse to her adornment, as if the bridled, jewelled mare and the woman have merged: cheeks framed by ornaments, a neck with strings of beads. Then a promise, in the plural: “We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.” The “we” may be the man speaking grandly, or the chorus joining in. Either way, praise turns into gift.

In verse 12 she takes up the theme of royalty again: “while the king was on his couch”. The word for couch, mēsab, suggests a reclining place at a banquet. While he reclines, her nard, a costly perfume from the Himalayas, fills the air. Then two compact, sensuous images. He is “a sachet of myrrh that lies all night between my breasts”: myrrh was carried by women in small bags under their clothing, so the man becomes the scent she wears against her skin through the night. And he is “a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi”, the lush oasis by the Dead Sea, a pocket of green and perfume in a barren landscape.

The exchange is balanced. He compares her to something powerful and adorned; she compares him to something small, fragrant and held close. The Song often lets the woman have the more intimate images. Notice also the movement of the verbs: he offers ornaments for her outside; she speaks of what lies between her breasts all night. His praise looks at her; hers takes him in.

words.note: From the root for friend or companion (rēa‘). It occurs nine times, always from his mouth to her, and is found almost nowhere else in the Bible. It joins desire and friendship: she is his darling and his equal. When she later calls him “my friend” (rē‘î, 5:16) she uses the same root, so each names the other as companion as well as lover.

A perfume oil from Nardostachys jatamansi, a plant of the Himalayas, carried by caravan and very expensive. It is a loanword, ultimately from Sanskrit. In Mark 14:3 and John 12:3 a woman breaks a jar of pure nard over Jesus, and the house fills with its scent, an echo many readers have heard of this verse.

words.gl: a bundle or sachet of myrrh
words.note: Myrrh (mōr) is a fragrant resin from Arabian and East African trees, used in perfume, anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), and burial. Ṣərôr is a small tied bundle or pouch. The verb “lies all night” (yālîn) is the ordinary word for lodging overnight. It is one of the Song’s most intimate images, made with complete simplicity.

Lawsonia inermis, whose white, sweet-scented flower clusters were prized, and whose leaves give the red dye for hands and hair. The word sounds like kōp̄er, ransom, which rabbinic readers did not fail to notice. The same plural, kəp̄ārîm, appears in 7:11, where this translation reads “henna blossoms” rather than “villages”.

history: Allegorical readers found Israel’s history in these lines. The Targum heard in the mare among Pharaoh’s chariots the crossing of the Red Sea, when Egypt’s horsemen were thrown into confusion. Rashi read the king on his couch as God at Sinai and the nard as Israel’s fragrance, though some rabbis noted uneasily that while Moses was on the mountain, the people made the golden calf, so the fragrance could be read as a bad smell. The sachet of myrrh resting between the breasts was read as the divine Presence dwelling between the two cherubim of the ark.

Christian interpreters loved the sachet of myrrh. Myrrh was associated with suffering and burial, and so Bernard of Clairvaux urged his monks to gather a little bundle of the sufferings of Christ and keep it near the heart. Medieval devotion to the Passion drew on this verse for centuries. Modern scholars, Othmar Keel among them, illustrate the horse imagery with ancient art of richly harnessed horses and the scent imagery with the spice trade, and they read the verses as a playful, sensual dialogue in which each lover answers the other’s praise.

life.love: His praise is a little extravagant and slightly odd; hers is tender and close. Couples often speak different languages of appreciation. The point is not to praise well but to praise at all, and to answer. When someone pays you a compliment that misses slightly, receive the intention. When you praise, be specific: not “you look nice”, but what you actually see.
life.body: Scent sits closer to memory and feeling than any other sense. She carries her beloved as a fragrance against her skin. Is there a smell that holds someone for you: a soap, a jumper, a kitchen? Give attention to scent today, your own and others’. The body remembers what the mind forgets.
life.inner: The sachet of myrrh was worn hidden, close to the heart, through the night. Every inner life needs something carried close in that way: a word, a memory, a prayer, a face. Not displayed, just kept. What do you carry close enough that it lasts through your nights?

passages.question: What or whom do I carry close to my heart through the night?

passages.title: Our bed is green

verses.t: Look at you: you are beautiful, my love. Look at you, how beautiful. Your eyes are doves.
Look at you: you are beautiful, my beloved, and how pleasant. Our bed is green with leaves.
The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are cypress.
I am a wildflower of the Sharon plain, a lily of the valleys.
Like a lily among thorns is my love among the young women.
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men. In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

passages.essence: The lovers praise each other in matching words, and their bed is the green earth under cedar beams. She calls herself a common wildflower; he makes her a lily among thorns; she answers that he is the apple tree whose shade she longed for.
reading: This passage is a duet. He says “Look at you: you are beautiful, my love”, and she answers with almost the same words, turned toward him: “Look at you: you are beautiful, my beloved.” Hebrew uses the masculine and feminine forms of the same adjective, yāp̄eh and yāp̄â, so the echo is exact. Few ancient texts give a woman the same language of beauty for a man that he gives to her. The Song does it from the start, and keeps doing it.

“Your eyes are doves” is the first of the Song’s many dove images. It may refer to the shape of the eyes, their soft grey shine, their quick movement, or the dove as an emblem of love; doves were the birds of the love goddess in the ancient Near East. The lovers’ home is then described: our bed is green, our beams are cedars, our rafters cypress. They are outside, lying on leaves under the trees, and calling it a house. Love makes architecture out of a forest.

In 2:1 she speaks modestly, perhaps playfully: “I am a wildflower of the Sharon plain, a lily of the valleys.” The Sharon was the coastal plain, where wildflowers grow in thousands; she is saying “I am just one of many.” He turns it at once: like a lily among thorns, so is she among the young women. What she offers as ordinary, he makes unique. The thorns are a strong word (ḥôḥîm, brambles), and the contrast is total.

She takes his form and answers in kind: like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is he among the young men. A fruit tree in a wild wood is both rare and nourishing. “In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat” renders a Hebrew phrase that piles desire and fulfilment together (ḥimmadtî wəyāšaḇtî, I delighted and I sat). Shade means protection from the noon sun she spoke of in 1:6; fruit sweet to the taste is unmistakably sensual. The apple tree will return twice more, in 2:5 and 8:5, as the place of their love.

words.note: The Song’s basic word for beauty, applied to her more than a dozen times and to him here. The repeated “look at you” is the particle hinnāk / hinnəḵā, “behold you”, a gesture of pointing, of really seeing. The parallel forms make the praise mutual. Elsewhere in the Bible yāp̄eh is used of Joseph, David and Absalom as well as Sarah, Rachel and Esther.

The exact flower is uncertain. Ancient translations guessed “flower”; modern guesses include crocus, asphodel, narcissus and the sea daffodil of the coast. The familiar “rose of Sharon” comes from older English versions and is almost certainly wrong. The sense is a common, beautiful wild bloom, one of many. Isaiah 35:1 uses it of the desert blossoming.

Probably a word borrowed from Egyptian, where the lotus was a symbol of love and renewal. It is the source of the name Susanna. It is not clear which flower is meant: white lily, red anemone, or lotus have all been proposed. In the Song lilies come to mark the place of lovemaking: he “grazes among the lilies” (2:16, 6:3).

The fruit may be the apple or the apricot; scholars disagree, and the apple of ancient Palestine was small. The word comes from a root for breathing out scent. In ancient love poetry, as in later folklore, apples are a fruit of love and fertility. That the apple became the forbidden fruit of Eden in Western art is partly due to Latin, where malum means both apple and evil.

history: The Targum takes the green bed and cedar beams as the Temple, built by Solomon from the cedars of Lebanon, where God and Israel meet. The Midrash reads the lily among thorns as Israel among the nations, beautiful amid hostility, and the apple tree among the trees of the forest as God, who alone among the gods offered Israel the Torah, which they longed for and sat in its shade.

In Christian tradition “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”, as the Latin has it, was often put in Christ’s mouth, and “rose of Sharon” and “lily of the valley” became titles of Jesus in hymns. The Church became the lily among thorns, persecuted by heretics and enemies. Mary was also called the lily among thorns. The apple tree’s shade became the shelter of the cross, and its fruit the Eucharist. Modern readers such as Ariel and Chana Bloch emphasise the poem’s pleasure in the outdoors: like other ancient lovers, these two meet in nature, away from the house, and make it their bedroom.

life.love: They say the same words to each other. Mutual praise is rare and precious: both people seeing and saying. If one of you always admires and the other always receives, try reversing it. And notice how he takes her modesty (“I’m just a wildflower”) and refuses it. Sometimes love’s work is to reject someone’s low opinion of themselves.
life.body: Their bed is green leaves under trees. Most of us live indoors, under artificial light. The body is an animal that loves shade, grass, air, a place to lie down outdoors. When did you last sit under a tree with nothing to do? The Song suggests that being in nature together is itself a form of intimacy.
life.inner: “In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat.” Desire, then rest. Many people know only the first half: wanting, striving, longing. The second half is the hardest: actually sitting down in the shade you longed for and letting yourself receive it. Where in your life are you allowed to rest, and do you?

passages.question: Where is the shade I long to sit in, and what keeps me from sitting down?

passages.title: His banner over me was love

verses.t: He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me was love.
Sustain me with raisin cakes, refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and by the does of the field: do not stir up, do not awaken love until it is ready.

passages.essence: She is brought to the house of wine under a banner of love, faint and asking to be fed with raisins and apples, held in his arms. Then, for the first time, she turns to the daughters of Jerusalem: do not awaken love until it is ready.
reading: “He brought me to the house of wine.” The phrase bêt hayyāyin can mean a banqueting hall, a tavern, or simply a place of celebration; here it is the place where love intoxicates. “His banner over me was love” is one of the Song’s most quoted lines and one of its least certain. The word deḡel usually means a military standard. Some scholars, following an Akkadian cognate, suggest “his intention” or “his look”: what he meant toward me, or the way he gazed at me, was love. The translation keeps “banner”, the old and vivid image of love raised over her like a flag, so that everyone can see whose side she is on.

Verse 5 is the first appearance of lovesickness, a theme as old as love poetry. She asks to be sustained with raisin cakes (’ăšîšôt, pressed cakes of dried grapes, eaten at festivals and, Hosea 3:1 suggests, at fertility rites) and refreshed with apples, “for I am sick with love.” The remedies are themselves love foods: she asks to be cured of desire with more of what causes it. Egyptian love songs have the same conceit: a lover is ill, and no doctor can help, only the beloved.

Verse 6 is an embrace, simple and complete: his left hand under her head, his right hand around her. It is the position of lovers lying together, and the verb in the second half (təḥabbəqēnî) can mean either “embraces me” or, as a wish, “let it embrace me”. The line is repeated in 8:3, near the end of the Song.

Then the refrain, which will come three times (here, 3:5, 8:4) and acts like a bar line in music. She makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear “by the gazelles and the does of the field”. In Hebrew these words, ṣəḇā’ôt and ’ayəlôt haśśādeh, sound very close to the divine titles “the Lord of hosts” (ṣəḇā’ôt) and “God Almighty” (’ēl šadday): an oath that playfully avoids God’s name while invoking the wild creatures of love instead. And the content: “do not stir up, do not awaken love until it is ready.” This could mean “do not disturb us now”, but most readers hear a general wisdom: love has its own time and cannot be forced. The woman most overwhelmed by desire is also the one who counsels patience.

words.gl: banner, standard; perhaps intention or gaze
words.note: In Numbers 1 and 2 deḡel is the banner of each tribe in the camp. The related verb appears in 5:10, where he is “standing out” (dāḡûl, as if bannered) among ten thousand, and in 6:4 and 6:10, “awesome as bannered hosts” (nidgālôt). So the military imagery is part of the Song’s vocabulary. The Akkadian-based alternative, “intention”, has support from scholars such as Marvin Pope, but the image of a banner fits the Song’s own echoes.

Ḥôlâ is the ordinary word for being ill or weak. ’Ahăḇâ is the general Hebrew word for love, used for love of God, of friends, of a spouse; it appears eleven times in the Song, more than in almost any other book. Lovesickness is a stock theme of Egyptian love poetry and of later Arabic, Persian and European love literature. She uses the phrase again in 5:8.

words.gl: I make you swear, I adjure you
words.note: A formal oath formula, used elsewhere for serious covenants. Here a young woman binds her friends by oath in the name of gazelles and does. The playful substitution for God’s titles is widely noted by scholars. Gazelles are emblems of love and grace throughout the Song; he is a gazelle in 2:9 and 8:14.

words.gl: until it is ready; until it pleases
words.note: Literally “until it desires” or “until it pleases”. The subject is love itself (hā’ahăḇâ, “the love”), not the beloved, which is why many translations read “until it is ready”: love has its own will and time. Others take the refrain to mean simply “until we are done”. The Hebrew allows both, and the poem’s three repetitions give the line the weight of a principle.

history: The Targum and Rashi read the house of wine as Sinai, where Israel was brought to receive the Torah, and the banner as the tribal standards of the camp in the wilderness, ordered around the tabernacle in love. The raisin cakes and apples became the words of the Torah that sustain a people faint with exile. The oath to the daughters of Jerusalem was read, in Talmudic tradition (Ketubot 110b–111a), as one of the oaths sworn by Israel not to force the end of exile before its time: do not awaken love, do not storm the gates of redemption. This became an important text in later debates about Zionism.

Christian readers saw the house of wine as the Church and the sacrament, and the wound of love as the soul’s longing for God. Origen speaks of being wounded by the arrow of divine love; Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross used “sick with love” for the pain and sweetness of mystical union. Bernard’s sermons dwell on the left and right hand: the left for God’s gifts in this life, the right for the joy to come. Modern commentators such as Michael V. Fox place the passage alongside Egyptian songs where the lovesick lover takes to bed and only the beloved’s visit can heal, and many read the refrain as the Song’s central piece of wisdom about desire and time.

life.love: “Do not awaken love until it is ready.” The woman who is most in love counsels patience. Love cannot be forced or rushed, in yourself or in another person. Whether you are hoping for someone, rebuilding trust, or waiting for a child to come back to you, the refrain asks for respect toward love’s own timing. It is not passivity, but trust.
life.body: She is faint, she asks to be fed, she is held. Desire is not only in the mind; it makes us weak, hungry, in need of holding. The embrace in verse 6 is simple: a hand under the head, an arm around. Many people go long stretches without being held. If you can, hold or be held today, without hurry and without agenda.
life.inner: To be “sick with love” is to admit how much you need. Spiritual traditions have long used this phrase for longing for God or meaning. Longing is not a fault to be fixed; it can be a sign of what you are made for. What are you sick for? Let the ache tell you something rather than rushing to cure it.

passages.question: What am I trying to awaken before it is ready, and what would it mean to trust its time?

passages.title: Arise and come away

verses.t: The voice of my beloved! Look, here he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.
My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Look, there he stands behind our wall, gazing in at the windows, peering through the lattice.
My beloved spoke and said to me: “Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
For look, the winter is past; the rains are over and gone.
Flowers appear in the land; the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
The fig tree ripens its first figs, and the vines in blossom give their scent. Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.”

passages.essence: The most famous spring song in the Bible: he comes bounding over the hills, stands at her wall, and calls her out into a world that has just come back to life. Love here is an invitation to leave shelter and step into the season that has arrived.
reading: The passage opens with a sound before a sight: “The voice of my beloved!” In Hebrew it is just two words, qôl dôdî, an exclamation rather than a sentence, like someone who hears a familiar step on the stairs. Then she sees him, and he is all motion: leaping over mountains, bounding over hills. The verbs are those of an animal, and she says so at once: he is like a gazelle or a young stag. In the Song the gazelle is the image of male vitality and freedom, quick, beautiful and hard to hold. He will come back to it at the very end (8:14).

Suddenly the motion stops. He stands “behind our wall”, looking in at the windows, peering through the lattice. The scene is almost comic and very tender: the swift animal of the hills has become a young man at a window. The house is hers, or her family’s; he is outside it. The whole Song plays with this boundary between inside and outside, the protected space of home and the open country where lovers can meet.

Then she reports his words, and the passage becomes a song within the song. “Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away” frames his speech at both ends (2:10, 2:13), like a refrain that opens and closes a door. Between the two calls he gives his reason: the winter is over. The Hebrew word for winter, sĕtāw, occurs only here in the Bible. The rains of the Levant fall from about October to April; when they stop, the hills turn green almost overnight. He lists the signs: flowers, singing, the turtledove (a migrant that returns in April), the first green figs, the vine in blossom with its faint sweet smell. Spring is not described from a distance; it is used as an argument. Everything else has woken up; why not you?

The final verse changes the image. She is now a dove hiding “in the clefts of the rock”, in the hiding places of the cliff. Rock doves nest in crevices in steep limestone, safe and almost invisible. He does not climb in after her. He asks to see her face and hear her voice. The request is gentle and specific: not possession, but presence. The repetition of “your voice… your face” in reverse order (face, voice; voice, face) is a small chiasm that wraps the request around her like an embrace.

Notice the shape of the whole: it begins with her hearing his voice and ends with him longing to hear hers. Love in the Song is mutual in this way again and again. One person calls; the other answers; and the poem lets us hear both.

words.gl: the voice of my beloved! / listen, my beloved!
words.note: Qôl means “voice” or “sound”, but at the start of a sentence it often works as an exclamation: “Listen!” (as in Isaiah 40:3, “A voice cries out”). Here both senses are present. She recognises him by sound before sight. The same two words open her night scene in 5:2, “Listen! My beloved is knocking”, where the story goes very differently.

words.gl: the time of singing / the time of pruning
words.note: Zāmîr can come from a root meaning “to sing” or from one meaning “to prune” vines. Older versions (the Greek, the Latin) chose pruning; most modern translators choose singing, since the next line is about the voice of the dove. The ambiguity is probably deliberate: spring is both the season of song and of tending the vines, and the Song loves words that do two things at once.

words.gl: and come away (literally: go, for yourself)
words.note: The same idiom God speaks to Abraham in Genesis 12:1, lek-lĕkā, “go, for yourself, from your land”. Here it is in the feminine. Readers have long heard the echo: a call to leave the familiar and go toward what is promised. The “for yourself” is a Hebrew way of adding emphasis and personal interest: go, and it will be for your own good.

The dove is his favourite name for her (2:14, 5:2, 6:9), and her eyes are doves (1:15, 4:1). In Near Eastern art the dove is the bird of the love goddess and a messenger of love. Here the image is precise: a wild rock dove, shy, nesting in cliffs. He calls the one he loves by the name of something beautiful that cannot be forced out of hiding.

history: Jewish tradition read this passage as the Exodus. In the Targum and in Song of Songs Rabbah, the beloved leaping over mountains is God “skipping” over the appointed time to bring Israel out of Egypt sooner than expected, and the winter that is past is the four hundred years of slavery. The lattice through which he peers is God watching over Israel in hiding. Because of this, the Song as a whole is read in synagogue at Passover, which falls in spring. The dove in the cleft of the rock became Israel trapped between the sea and Pharaoh’s army, asked by God to let her voice be heard in prayer.

Christian readers heard the voice of Christ calling the soul out of the winter of sin. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa saw the lattice as the prophets and the law, through which Christ was seen only partly before the incarnation. Bernard of Clairvaux preached on the “clefts of the rock” as the wounds of Christ, where the soul hides safely, an image that became a commonplace of medieval devotion. Modern scholars, Michael V. Fox and Othmar Keel among them, point instead to the ancient Egyptian love songs, where the lover waits outside the girl’s house, and to the simple realism of a Palestinian spring.

life.love: Love often arrives as a voice before it is a face: a message, a step, a way of saying your name. Here the lover does not drag the beloved out; he gives reasons, names the season, and asks. Is there someone in your life who is calling you out of a long winter, and are you answering? Or is there someone you need to invite, not pressure, by naming what has changed and asking to see their face?
life.body: This passage is full of the senses at the change of season: the smell of blossoming vines, the sound of the dove, green figs, the light on new grass. Desire in the Song is never abstract; it lives in a body that notices the world. Go outside at the turn of a season and let it actually reach you. The body that can feel spring is the same body that can feel love.
life.inner: Winter is real, and the passage does not deny it. But there comes a time when the rains are over and staying inside is no longer safety but habit. “Rise up and come away” can be heard as a call from God, from your own deeper life, or from the moment itself. What would it mean to admit that a season in you has ended?

passages.question: What winter in my life is already over, while I am still living as though it were not?

passages.title: The little foxes

verses.t: Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom.
My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.
Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the cleft mountains.

passages.essence: A riddle about little foxes, a vow of belonging, and a night that lasts until the day breathes. Three short verses that hold the Song’s great refrain: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
reading: The first verse is one of the strangest in the Song. Who says it, and to whom? “Catch the foxes for us” is in the plural, and the verb is masculine plural, so it seems addressed to a group, perhaps the brothers who made her keep the vineyards (1:6), perhaps anyone listening. Many scholars think it is a fragment of a folk song or a teasing rhyme; the Hebrew is full of repeated sounds (šû‘ālîm šû‘ālîm qĕṭannîm, “foxes, little foxes”). Foxes, or jackals (the word covers both), really did damage vineyards, digging, gnawing young vines and eating grapes.

In the Song, though, the vineyard is never only a vineyard. She has already called her own body “my vineyard” (1:6). Vineyards “in blossom” are vineyards at their most vulnerable and most promising. So the foxes are often read as whatever might spoil young love before it ripens: rivals, gossip, the predatory young men of the village, or simply the small daily things that eat at intimacy. Others hear a playful double meaning, the foxes as the lovers themselves, eager to get into the vineyard. The verse lets both readings stand.

Then comes the line that is the heart of the Song: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” In Hebrew it is four short words, dôdî lî wa’ănî lô, perfectly balanced. It returns twice more, each time slightly changed. In 6:3 the order is reversed: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” In 7:10 it becomes “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” The movement across the book, from “he is mine” toward “I am his” and finally “his desire is for me”, has been read as a growth in love from having to giving to being desired. “He grazes among the lilies” is a pastoral picture with a clear erotic undertone: the lilies are associated with her body (4:5) and her lips are his lilies in reverse (5:13).

The last verse is an invitation for the night. “Until the day breathes and the shadows flee” probably means the cool breeze before dawn, when shadows dissolve in the first light, though some read it as the evening wind when shadows lengthen. Either way, she asks him to be the gazelle again on “the cleft mountains”, harê beter. Beter may be a place name (Bether, near Jerusalem), or it may mean “separation”, “cleft”. Many readers take the cleft mountains as an image of her own body. The same line returns, transformed, in 4:6 and 8:14.

words.note: The word names both animals, which look alike to a farmer. Samson used three hundred of them to burn the Philistines’ fields (Judges 15:4). In Egyptian love poetry and in later Arabic poetry, the fox can be a figure for the sly young man. Here the “little” foxes matter: not wolves or lions, but small, quick creatures that do damage while no one is watching.

words.gl: my beloved is mine, and I am his
words.note: The formula echoes covenant language, “I will be your God and you will be my people” (Jeremiah 7:23), but in the intimate register of two people. Its balance is the point: neither belongs to the other more. In a world where women were often spoken of as possessions, the Song puts the language of mutual belonging in a woman’s mouth, three times.

The verb pûaḥ means to blow or breathe, as a breeze does. It is the same root she uses when she calls the winds to “breathe on my garden” (4:16). The day itself is imagined as something alive that breathes. Translators split between dawn and evening; the poem’s nights of love suggest dawn, when lovers part.

history: For the rabbis the foxes were Israel’s enemies, in the Targum the Amalekites who attacked Israel in the wilderness, and in Song of Songs Rabbah the small sins that ruin a people. Rashi took them as the enemies who harried Israel as soon as it left Egypt. “My beloved is mine and I am his” became a beloved line of Jewish piety: its initial letters in the reversed form of 6:3 spell Elul, the month of repentance before the New Year, and the verse is still read as God and Israel turning toward each other in that season. It is also engraved inside many Jewish wedding rings.

In Christian teaching, from Origen through Bernard of Clairvaux, the little foxes became heresies and small temptations that spoil the vineyard of the Church or of the soul; Bernard devoted whole sermons to them, warning especially against subtle faults that look like virtues. Teresa of Ávila and others used the mutual belonging of 2:16 as the clearest expression of union with God. Modern readers such as Ariel and Chana Bloch hear in the foxes a teasing song between lovers, and in 2:17 a frankly erotic invitation.

life.love: Big crises rarely ruin a relationship by themselves; little foxes do. A habit of not listening, a joke that wounds, a phone at the table, a resentment never named. Love in blossom needs guarding, and guarding is a shared task: “catch them for us”. What small thing is gnawing at a relationship you care about, and could you name it together, without blame?
life.body: “My beloved is mine and I am his” is spoken by a body as much as a mind: it is the feeling of being at home in someone’s presence, of touch that is welcome both ways. Belonging is not the same as being owned. Notice where in your body you feel trust and where you feel guarded. Mutual belonging is felt before it is understood.
life.inner: The night in this passage is not frightening; it is an invitation to stay until the light comes. Inner life also has its nights, when you can only keep watch and wait for the day to breathe. Can you trust that the shadows flee on their own schedule, and that your part is only to stay?

passages.question: What little foxes are slipping into the vineyards I care most about?

passages.title: The search by night

verses.t: On my bed, night after night, I sought the one my soul loves. I sought him, but did not find him.
“I will rise now and go about the city, through the streets and the squares; I will seek the one my soul loves.” I sought him, but did not find him.
The watchmen found me as they went about the city. “Have you seen the one my soul loves?”
I had barely passed them when I found the one my soul loves. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother’s house, into the room of the one who conceived me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and by the does of the field: do not stir up, do not awaken love until it is ready.

passages.essence: She lies awake missing him, gets up and searches the dark city, asks the watchmen, and finds him. A short story of desire that will not wait, told like a dream, ending with the refrain that love must not be hurried.
reading: The scene begins in bed and in the plural: “on my bed, night after night” (balêlôt, literally “in the nights”). This is not one restless evening but a longing that has gone on. The phrase that dominates the passage, “the one my soul loves”, comes four times in four verses. She never names him; the phrase is his name. In Hebrew nepeš, “soul”, is not a ghostly inner self but the whole living person, throat, breath and appetite included. To love with the nepeš is to love with everything that keeps you alive.

The searching is told with almost hypnotic repetition: I sought him, but did not find him; I will seek; I sought him, but did not find him. Then she does something remarkable for a young woman in the ancient world: she gets up and goes out alone into the city at night, through the streets and squares. The poem does not comment on the risk. It simply lets her desire carry her past every convention. Many readers sense the logic of a dream here: the sudden change of place, the watchmen who appear, the question with no answer recorded, the beloved found just around the corner.

The watchmen “found” her, the same verb she has been using for her failed search; she is found by the wrong people. She asks them, abruptly, “Have you seen the one my soul loves?”, as if everyone must know whom she means. They do not answer. In the parallel night scene of 5:2–8 the watchmen will beat her; here they are merely useless. Then, “I had barely passed them”, she finds him, and the verbs turn strong and physical: I held him, I would not let him go, I brought him in.

Where does she bring him? Into her mother’s house, “into the room of the one who conceived me”. The mother’s house appears again in 8:2 and is unusual in the Bible, where households are normally called “the father’s house”. It suggests a woman’s world: the place of birth, intimacy and safety, and perhaps of marriage arrangements made by mothers (compare Genesis 24:28 and Ruth 1:8). The search moves from the bed, out to the city, and back into the most intimate room of all.

Then the refrain from 2:7 returns word for word: she makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear not to stir up or awaken love until it is ready. Coming straight after this urgent night, the warning has weight. Love, once awakened, does exactly this: it gets you out of bed and into the streets. Do not start it lightly.

words.note: Nepeš is the throat, the breath, the appetite, the life itself (Genesis 2:7: the man became a living nepeš). So the phrase is close to “the one I love with my whole being”. It appears first in 1:7 and then four times here, making this passage the Song’s portrait of pure longing. It is also echoed in the command to love God “with all your nepeš” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

words.gl: I sought him, but did not find him
words.note: The pairing of “seek” and “find” is everywhere in biblical wisdom and prayer: “you will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13); Wisdom says “those who seek me diligently find me” (Proverbs 8:17). The Song turns the familiar pair upside down: she seeks and does not find, twice, before finding. The repetition makes the waiting audible.

Rare in the Hebrew Bible, which usually speaks of the “father’s house” as the unit of family and inheritance. It occurs in the stories of Rebekah (Genesis 24:28) and in Ruth (1:8), both in contexts of marriage. Carol Meyers has argued that it points to a women’s domain with its own authority. In the Song it is where love is brought home.

words.gl: do not stir up (literally: if you stir up)
words.note: An oath formula: “I make you swear… if you stir up” means “that you will not”. The verbs ‘ûr (stir, rouse) and ‘ôrēr (awaken) are a wordplay on the same root, as in English “do not wake or waken”. The refrain falls at 2:7, 3:5 and 8:4, dividing the Song into movements. Its sense is debated: do not arouse love artificially, or do not disturb lovers until they are done.

history: Rabbinic readers took the night as Israel’s long wandering in the wilderness or its exile, when God seemed absent. In the Targum, the bed is the nights in the desert under the cloud, the watchmen are Moses and Aaron, and the mother’s house is the Tabernacle or the Temple, where God’s presence was brought to dwell. Rashi follows this closely. The refrain becomes an oath not to try to force the end of exile before God’s time, a reading the Talmud (Ketubot 111a) uses to discourage mass return to the land by force.

Christian mystics loved this passage. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa saw the soul searching for God in the night of this world; Gregory insisted that the finding is only the beginning, since God is always more than any finding. Augustine’s line “you were within, and I was outside, seeking you” is close to its spirit. John of the Cross built his poem “The Dark Night” on this scene: the soul slips out of the sleeping house at night, guided only by the fire in its heart. Modern scholars note the dreamlike structure, and J. Cheryl Exum reads the night scenes as the poet’s way of showing desire through absence.

life.love: Longing is part of love, not a failure of it. This passage honours the nights when the other is not there, and the courage of going to look instead of waiting to be found. Is there someone whose absence you feel, whom you could seek out, call, or walk toward, even if it feels unconventional? Love sometimes asks you to get out of bed and into the street.
life.body: Notice how bodily the passage is: lying awake, getting up, walking the streets, holding on and not letting go. Longing lives in the body as restlessness, sleeplessness and a kind of hunger. Rather than numbing it, the Song lets it move her. What does your body do with longing? Can you feel it without running from it or being run by it?
life.inner: Many spiritual traditions know nights when what you love most seems absent and the official guardians, the watchmen, have no answer. The passage does not say the absence is a punishment. It says to keep seeking. The finding comes “barely past” the people who could not help. What are you seeking that the usual authorities cannot show you?

passages.question: Whom or what does my soul love so much that I would get up in the night to look for it?

passages.title: Solomon’s carriage

verses.t: Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with every powder of the merchant?
Look: it is Solomon’s couch! Sixty warriors surround it, of the warriors of Israel,
all of them wearing swords, all trained for battle, each with his sword at his thigh against the terrors of the night.
King Solomon made himself a carriage of wood from Lebanon.
He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its inside was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
Go out, daughters of Zion, and look at King Solomon, at the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of his heart’s joy.

passages.essence: Out of the desert comes a cloud of perfume: Solomon’s carriage, guarded by sixty warriors, lined with love, carrying the king to his wedding. A procession song that turns the lovers’ day into a royal festival.
reading: The voice changes. After the woman’s intimate night, someone, perhaps the poet, perhaps a chorus, calls out like a spectator at a parade: “Who is this coming up from the wilderness?” The Hebrew word for “this” is feminine (zō’t), which has puzzled readers since what follows is Solomon’s couch. The question may refer to the carriage itself (a feminine noun) or to the bride who rides in it. The same question is asked of the woman in 6:10 and 8:5, which suggests that she is in view here too.

What appears first is smoke: columns of it, perfumed with myrrh, frankincense and “every powder of the merchant”, the expensive imported spices. The wilderness is the dry land east and south of Jerusalem; a procession coming up from it is coming home. The image of smoke from the desert also recalls the pillar of cloud that led Israel through the wilderness, an echo later readers seized on.

Then the object comes into view. Two different words are used: miṭṭâ (3:7), a couch or litter for carrying a person, and ’appiryôn (3:9), a rare word found only here, probably a palanquin or sedan chair, possibly borrowed from Greek phoreion or from Persian. The sixty warriors, twice David’s famous thirty (2 Samuel 23), with swords at their thighs “against the terrors of the night”, are part of the pageantry. In the ancient world the night before a wedding was believed to be dangerous, haunted by demons who envied the couple (compare the demon in Tobit 8). The guards give the scene a feeling of protected joy.

The materials are luxurious: cedar from Lebanon, silver posts, a gold back, a seat of purple, the costliest dye in the ancient world. The inside is “inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem”. The Hebrew phrase is odd; some scholars emend ’ahăbâ (love) to a similar word for leather or ebony. But “inlaid with love” fits the Song perfectly: the women of the city have lined the carriage with love, or with love scenes worked in embroidery.

The final verse names the occasion: Solomon’s wedding day, the crown his mother set on him, “the day of his heart’s joy”. This is the only explicit wedding in the Song, and it sits almost exactly at its centre. Most scholars think the lovers are not literally Solomon and his bride; the poet borrows the most splendid wedding imaginable to say what this love feels like from inside. In village weddings in the Near East, as Wetzstein noted in nineteenth-century Syria, bride and groom were crowned and called king and queen for the week.

words.note: The feminine form signals a woman, though the next lines describe a carriage. The formula recurs at 6:10 and 8:5 and in each case points to the woman as a sudden, astonishing appearance. ‘Ālâ, “go up”, is the normal verb for travel to Jerusalem, and for incense smoke rising, so the sense of arrival and of offering is doubled.

Found only here. Its origin is debated: a loan from Greek phoreion (a litter), from Sanskrit or Persian, or from an Egyptian word. Because a Greek origin would imply a late date, the word is part of the long argument about when the Song was written. Rabbinic readers, unsure what it was, linked it to the Temple or the Tabernacle.

Paḥad is dread, sudden fear. The phrase recalls Psalm 91:5, “you will not fear the terror of the night”. Ancient readers believed night, especially a wedding night, was the hour of hostile spirits. The warriors are there to make the joy safe. The same word “nights” (lêlôt) opened 3:1, linking the woman’s anxious night to this protected one.

words.gl: on the day of his wedding
words.note: Ḥătunnâ, “wedding”, occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Its root gives ḥātān, bridegroom. The verse is the reason the Song has always been sung and read at weddings, and why many interpreters, ancient and modern, have read the whole book as wedding poetry, even though most of its love scenes are not presented as married love.

history: The Targum and Rashi read the procession as Israel coming up from the wilderness after the Exodus, led by the pillar of cloud and fire, and the palanquin as the Tabernacle or Solomon’s Temple, built of cedar from Lebanon and gold. The sixty warriors became the sixty letters in the Priestly Blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) or the priests and Levites guarding the sanctuary, and the wedding day became the giving of the Torah at Sinai or the dedication of the Temple. The Mishnah (Taanit 4:8) itself reads “the day of his wedding” as Sinai and “the day of his heart’s joy” as the building of the Temple.

Christian interpreters saw Christ the king and his bride the Church. Some medieval writers took the crown his mother gave him as the human nature Christ received from Mary, and even the crown of thorns. Modern scholarship has been more interested in history and form: is this a fragment of a royal wedding song, like Psalm 45? J. G. Wetzstein’s account of Syrian village weddings, where the threshing sledge became a royal throne for the “king” and “queen”, was enormously influential, and Marvin Pope collected parallels from many cultures.

life.love: Love makes ordinary people royalty for a day; this is what weddings are for. The passage invites you to treat the people you love with ceremony sometimes: to mark their days, to dress up for them, to make a procession of a homecoming. When did you last make someone feel crowned?
life.body: Smoke, perfume, purple cloth, cedar and gold: the passage is a feast for the senses, and it suggests that love deserves beauty. Joy also needs safety, which the warriors provide. Notice what helps your body feel both festive and safe at once: certain clothes, a place, a ritual, the presence of people who guard you.
life.inner: The night is still full of terrors; the procession goes through it anyway, guarded. Spiritual life is not the absence of fear but a joy that has been given protection: practices, friends, words that stand around you with swords drawn. What guards your joy against the terrors of the night?

passages.question: What in my life deserves a procession, and who would walk in it with me?

passages.title: You are beautiful, my love

verses.t: Look at you: you are beautiful, my love. Look at you, how beautiful. Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes coming up from the washing: each one has its twin, and not one of them is missing.
Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheek behind your veil is like a half of a pomegranate.
Your neck is like the tower of David, built in courses: a thousand shields hang on it, all the round shields of warriors.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.
Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.
You are beautiful through and through, my love; there is no flaw in you.

passages.essence: He describes her, from her eyes down, in images taken from the land around them: goats on a hillside, washed ewes, a pomegranate, a tower, two fawns. The first full song of praise for the body in the Bible, and it ends: there is no flaw in you.
reading: This is the first of the Song’s descriptive poems about the body. Scholars call this kind of poem a wasf, an Arabic word meaning “description”, borrowed from the Syrian wedding songs that J. G. Wetzstein recorded in the nineteenth century, in which bride and groom were praised part by part. There are four in the Song: three of her (4:1–7, 6:4–10, 7:1–5) and one of him, spoken by her (5:10–16). This one moves downward, from eyes to breasts, framed at each end by praise of her whole beauty (4:1 and 4:7).

The images are surprising, and they are meant to be. Her hair is “like a flock of goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead”. Palestinian goats were mostly black; seen from a distance, a herd moving down a hillside in the evening light ripples like long dark hair falling over shoulders. Her teeth are like shorn ewes coming up from the washing: white, clean, all in pairs, none missing, which in a world without dentistry was real praise. The poet is not saying she looks like a goat. He is saying that the feeling of seeing her is like the feeling of seeing these things: abundance, motion, freshness, life.

Othmar Keel, studying ancient Near Eastern art, argued that many of the images carry symbolic weight beyond appearance. Doves were messengers of love and birds of the love goddess, so “your eyes are doves” means her glances carry desire. The tower of David hung with shields, a fortified tower decorated with the shields of heroes, suggests her neck is proud, upright and adorned with necklaces, but also strong and unconquerable. The two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among lilies, are images of tenderness, youth and life; in Egyptian and Near Eastern art, young animals among lotus flowers are symbols of renewal.

The pomegranate is one of the Song’s key fruits. “Your cheek behind your veil is like a half of a pomegranate”: the word for cheek, raqqâ, may mean temple or brow; the split pomegranate shows its red interior and glistening seeds. The colour of her skin flushed behind the veil, and a hint of fertility and sweetness, are both present. The veil, mentioned twice here, is not a sign of shyness alone; it adds mystery to what he sees.

Verse 6 suddenly turns from description to intention. He takes up her words from 2:17 (“until the day breathes and the shadows flee”) and declares that he will go to “the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense”. After a downward journey through her body, the image of fragrant hills is easy to read. Then the closing line gathers everything: you are all beautiful, my love, kullāk yāpâ, “all of you is beautiful”, and there is no blemish (mûm) in you. Mûm is the word used for the physical defects that disqualified a sacrificial animal or a priest. To his eyes she is perfect in the way only holy things are.

words.gl: description; a poem praising the body
words.note: Not a Hebrew word but the scholarly name for this form, from Arabic. Wetzstein, a Prussian consul in Damascus, described village weddings in which songs praising the bride’s body were sung during a week of feasting. Since then the term has been used for the descriptive poems of the Song. Similar songs exist in ancient Egyptian love poetry, which Michael V. Fox has compared closely with the Song.

The key word of the passage, and one of the commonest in the Song (about a dozen times). It opens and closes this poem: “you are beautiful… you are beautiful through and through”. Biblical narrative uses it for Sarah, Rachel, David and Esther, almost always briefly. Only the Song lingers over beauty, saying it again and again as an act of attention.

A rare word (here, 4:3, 6:7 and Isaiah 47:2). Some older translations thought it meant hair or locks; most now take it as a veil. In Isaiah, removing the ṣammâ is a sign of humiliation; here it is a sign of a woman seen partly, intimately, with the face framed. The eyes seen through the veil are more striking, not less.

In Leviticus a mûm disqualifies an animal from sacrifice (22:20) and a priest from serving at the altar (21:17). Absalom was praised as having no mûm “from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head” (2 Samuel 14:25). The lover borrows this weighty word to say that she is whole and without defect, a gift worthy of an altar.

history: The allegorical tradition worked hard on these images, mapping each part of the body onto a part of the community of faith. In the Targum, her eyes are the leaders and sages of Israel, her teeth the priests and Levites who eat the offerings, her neck the head of the court, the tower of David the learning of the Torah, and her two breasts the two messiahs, son of David and son of Ephraim, or Moses and Aaron. Christian readers did the same for the Church: the teeth were preachers who “chew” the word for others, the twins were the two commandments of love, the breasts the Old and New Testaments.

Modern scholars have been more interested in the poetic method. Some, like Marvin Pope, emphasised the erotic and mythic background; others, like Othmar Keel, used ancient art to show what the images symbolised; Robert Alter has written about how the Song’s metaphors work by sudden leaps between the body and the landscape, so that the woman and the land of Israel seem to merge. Feminist critics have debated whether the wasf objectifies the woman or celebrates her; J. Cheryl Exum notes that the woman also describes the man in the same way, which keeps the gaze mutual.

life.love: To be loved is, in part, to be looked at with delight. When did you last tell someone what you find beautiful in them, in detail, not in general? The wasf teaches the art of specific praise. You can practise it in words, but also in attention: noticing a person carefully is already a form of love.
life.body: This poem is a direct answer to the shame many people feel about their bodies. It does not compare her to an ideal; it compares her to living things in a real landscape, and it ends “there is no flaw in you”. Try looking at your own body, or a loved one’s, through these eyes: not as a list of defects, but as a landscape full of life.
life.inner: Many traditions say that God looks at each person with the gaze of this poem, a gaze that sees wholeness where we see blemish. Whether or not you believe that, you can learn to look at yourself with less judgement and more wonder. What would change if you heard “there is no flaw in you” said to you, and believed it?

passages.question: Whom have I never told, in detail, what I find beautiful in them?

passages.title: My sister, my bride

verses.t: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Come down from the peak of Amana, from the top of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
You have stolen my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one bead of your necklace.
How beautiful your love is, my sister, my bride! How much better your love than wine, and the scent of your oils than any spice!
Your lips drip honey, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your clothes is like the scent of Lebanon.

passages.essence: He calls her down from the high, wild mountains of the north and names her for the first time “bride” and “sister”. One glance from her has undone him, and he answers her first words of the Song with his own: your love is better than wine.
reading: The passage opens far from any garden. Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon are the great mountains of the north: Amana is the range behind Damascus (its river, the Abana, is the one Naaman the Syrian preferred to the Jordan in 2 Kings 5:12), and Senir, Deuteronomy 3:9 tells us, is what the Amorites called Hermon. These are snow peaks, haunts of lions and leopards, the edge of the known world. He does not picture her as a village girl but as a creature of the heights, beautiful and a little dangerous, at home among predators. Othmar Keel noted that ancient Near Eastern art shows goddesses standing on lions or flanked by them; the man’s imagination lifts her into that company. The call to “come down” is a call from remoteness into nearness.

Even the verbs shimmer. “Come down” (tāšûrî) can also be heard as “look” or “gaze” (from the verb šûr), so the line may mean both: descend from the peak, and look out from it. And the opening “with me” (’ittî) was read by the old Greek translation as “come” (’ētî), which makes the first words an even more insistent summons. The repetition, “from Lebanon… from Lebanon”, has the rhythm of someone calling across a distance.

Then the tone changes from summons to confession. “You have stolen my heart” renders a single rare Hebrew verb built on the word for heart. He is not in control: one glance, one bead of her necklace, is enough. The smallness of the detail is the point. Love does not need the whole picture; it is caught by a fragment, a flash of the eyes, a glint of jewellery at the throat.

In verse 10 he says to her almost exactly what she said to him in 1:2–3: your love is better than wine, the scent of your oils is sweeter than any spice. The Song is built on these returns. Desire flows both ways, and each lover borrows the other’s words. Verse 11 brings honey and milk: her lips drip with the honey of the comb, and honey and milk are under her tongue. Any Israelite ear would hear “a land flowing with milk and honey”, the old promise of the good land (Exodus 3:8). The woman is described like the promised land itself: the place of plenty that one longs to reach. The scent of her clothes is the scent of Lebanon, its cedars and resin, so the mountains he called her from cling to her still.

Here too the word “bride” (kallâ) enters the Song. It appears six times between 4:8 and 5:1 and nowhere else, gathered around the garden poem that follows. Whatever their formal status, in this stretch of the Song they speak as people who belong to each other.

words.note: The everyday word for a bride, and also for a daughter-in-law. In the Song it is concentrated in 4:8–5:1, six times in a few verses, and then disappears. Some readers take it as evidence of a wedding setting; others as a term of endearment, the way lovers in many languages call each other “wife” or “husband” before or apart from any ceremony. Either way, it marks this section as the Song’s most intimate.

Not a hint of incest, but the language of love poetry. In the Egyptian love songs of the New Kingdom, which Michael V. Fox showed to be the Song’s closest relatives, lovers regularly call each other “my sister” and “my brother”. The word claims a kinship deeper than romance: you are as near to me as family, as much my own. In 8:1 the woman wishes, playfully, that he really were her brother.

A verb made from lēb, “heart”, found only here and in a proverb in Job 11:12. It might mean “you have made my heart beat”, “you have given me courage” or, more likely, “you have taken my heart away”. English has the same double idiom: to hearten and to dishearten. Whatever its exact force, the man is describing what love does to his centre.

Named three times in these four verses. The name sounds like lābān, “white” (for its snows), and like lĕbōnâ, “frankincense” (4:6, 4:14). In the Song Lebanon stands for height, fragrance and grandeur: cedar beams (1:17), Solomon’s carriage (3:9), the streams of 4:15, his bearing in 5:15. To say her clothes smell of Lebanon is to wrap her in all of it.

history: The Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase read in synagogues, hears in “Lebanon” a familiar code for the Temple (its cedar timbers came from there), and takes the passage as God speaking to Israel, the congregation called “bride”. Rashi, in the eleventh century, reads “with me from Lebanon” with great tenderness: when you went into exile, I went with you; when you return, I return with you. The mountains of lions and leopards become the kingdoms that oppressed Israel, from which God promises to bring her home.

Christian readers made the bride the Church or the individual soul, called upward and then inward. Origen saw in the mountains the stages of ascent and in the single glance the undivided gaze of a soul that has learned to look only at God. In the twelfth century Rupert of Deutz wrote the first commentary to read the whole Song of the Virgin Mary, and “my sister, my bride” became one of the great Marian phrases of the Middle Ages. Modern scholars, following Fox, set the “sister” language beside the Egyptian songs and read the passage as human love poetry of high artistry: a summons, a confession, an exchange of praise.

life.love: He uses her own words back to her. Something deep happens when we tell the people we love what they first told us, when the praise goes both ways. Notice where in your closest relationships the words of love flow only in one direction, and what it might take to return them.
life.body: One glance, one bead of a necklace: attraction often lives in the smallest details. You do not need to take in everything at once. Practise seeing one thing in a person you love, the way they hold a cup or turn their head, and letting it be enough to move you.
life.inner: The call comes down from the heights: come with me. Many traditions describe the spiritual life as a descent as well as an ascent, from lofty and distant ideals into nearness, into an ordinary room. Where are you living on a remote peak, admired but alone, when you are being invited closer?

passages.question: Who has stolen your heart with one glance, and have you told them?

passages.title: A garden locked

verses.t: A garden locked is my sister, my bride: a spring locked, a fountain sealed.
Your channels are an orchard of pomegranates with every choice fruit, henna with nard,
nard and saffron, sweet cane and cinnamon, with every tree of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices.
You are a fountain in the garden, a well of living water, streams flowing down from Lebanon.
Awake, north wind; come, south wind! Breathe on my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come into his garden and eat its choice fruits.
I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spice, I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk.
Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love.

passages.essence: The centre of the Song: he praises her as a locked garden full of every spice in the world; she opens it and invites him in; he enters and rejoices. A voice blesses them: eat, drink, be drunk with love.
reading: Everything in the Song has been leading to this garden. He calls her “a garden locked… a spring locked, a fountain sealed”. In a dry land, a walled garden with its own spring was the most precious thing a wealthy household could own, kept locked against intruders and thieves. The image is of something private, guarded, full of life, and not yet open. Most interpreters read it as her sexuality, which belongs to her and is opened only by her choice. The tone is not possessive but awed: she is a hidden source of water in a desert world.

Then the garden overflows. He lists pomegranates, henna, nard, saffron, sweet cane, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh and aloes. No real garden in Israel ever grew all of these. Nard came from the Himalayas, cinnamon from South or Southeast Asia, frankincense and myrrh from Arabia and the Horn of Africa. The list is a dream of every perfume of the known world in one place, the stock of a fabulous merchant. Several of them, cinnamon, sweet cane and myrrh, are also ingredients in the holy anointing oil of the Tabernacle (Exodus 30:23–24), so the garden carries a scent of the sacred as well as the sensual. In verse 15 the locked spring becomes “a well of living water, streams flowing down from Lebanon”: what was sealed is now abundant and flowing.

Verse 16 is the turning point of the whole book, and she speaks it. She calls on the north wind and the south wind to blow on the garden so that its fragrance spreads, and then she changes one small word: the garden is “my garden” in the first line and “his garden” in the second. The lock is opened from the inside. Nothing is taken; it is given.

His answer in 5:1 is in the Hebrew perfect tense, the tense of completed action: I have come, I have gathered, I have eaten, I have drunk. Myrrh with spice, honeycomb with honey, wine with milk: everything is enjoyed together, in pairs, without hurry. The word for “gathered” (’ārîtî) is used elsewhere only of passers by plucking the grapes of an unprotected vineyard (Psalm 80:12), but here the gathering is welcome. Readers have long noticed that this moment stands near the very middle of the Song.

Then an unnamed voice speaks to the lovers, or to their guests: “Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love.” Some hear the daughters of Jerusalem, some a chorus of wedding guests, some the poet stepping forward to bless what has happened. The last word, dōdîm, can mean “lovers” or “lovemaking”, so the line is both a toast to the couple and a blessing on love itself. Phyllis Trible read the whole Song as a return to Eden: here is a garden with rivers, fruit and eating, and this time the eating brings joy rather than shame.

words.note: Gan is the word used for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8). Nā‘ûl, “locked” or “barred”, is used of doors bolted shut (Judges 3:23). Together they make the most influential single image in the Song’s afterlife: the hortus conclusus, the enclosed garden of medieval art. In the poem itself the lock matters because she is the one who opens it, in 4:16.

A loanword from Old Persian, meaning a walled park. It occurs only three times in the Bible (here, Ecclesiastes 2:5, Nehemiah 2:8) and is one of the clues that the Song in its present form dates from the Persian period or later. Through Greek paradeisos it became our word “paradise”. In later Jewish tradition pardēs became a name for the inner garden of mystical knowledge.

From the root šlḥ, “to send out”. It can mean the shoots a plant sends out, which suits an orchard, or the channels that send water out, which suits the spring and fountain around it (compare the pool of Shelah in Nehemiah 3:15). This rendering keeps “channels” to hold the garden and the water together. Many readers sense a bodily meaning as well. The word is unique here, and no translation captures all of it.

“Living water” is running water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern. Proverbs 5:15–18 uses the same picture of a man’s own wife: drink water from your own well, let your fountain be blessed. Jeremiah 2:13 calls God “the fountain of living water”. The phrase lets the Song speak at once of a woman’s body, of fidelity and of the source of life.
