history: For Jewish interpreters the locked garden is Israel’s faithfulness. Song of Songs Rabbah reads it of the Israelite women in Egypt who kept themselves from their oppressors, and the Targum reads 4:16 to 5:1 of the Temple: the winds are the gathering of the exiles, and “I have come into my garden” is God entering the sanctuary to accept its offerings. The word pardēs had a long second life. The Talmud (Hagigah 14b) tells of four sages who “entered the pardēs”, a garden of mystical vision, of whom only Rabbi Akiva came out unharmed; medieval Jewish scholars later used PaRDeS as an acronym for the four levels of reading scripture: plain, allusive, homiletic and secret.

Christian writers from Ambrose and Jerome onward made the enclosed garden and sealed fountain a figure of Mary’s virginity, and the hortus conclusus became a favourite scene in late medieval painting: the Virgin seated in a walled garden of flowers, sometimes with a fountain and a unicorn. Others read the garden as the Church, watered by the fountain of baptism, or as the soul in which Christ walks. Modern scholars mostly read the passage as the Song’s great celebration of sexual union, given in images rather than description, and they note how carefully the poem gives the woman the decisive voice.

life.love: The garden is opened from inside, by her invitation. Lasting intimacy grows where each person is free to say yes in their own time. Think about the places in your relationships where you push at a locked gate, and where you could instead make it safe for the other to open it.
life.body: Myrrh with spice, honeycomb with honey, wine with milk: everything is savoured slowly, in pairs. Pleasure in the Song is never rushed or furtive. Try receiving one good thing today with full attention, letting taste and scent and touch be complete before you move on.
life.inner: Every person has an enclosed garden, an inner life that is not for everyone. That privacy is not a fault to overcome; it is where the living water is. Guard what is sacred in you, and notice whom you would truly want to invite in.

passages.question: What in you is a garden locked, and who, if anyone, holds the key?

passages.title: I slept, but my heart was awake

verses.t: I was asleep, but my heart was awake. Listen! My beloved is knocking. “Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is drenched with dew, my hair with the drops of the night.”
“I have taken off my robe; must I put it on again? I have washed my feet; must I dirty them?”
My beloved put his hand in through the opening, and my whole being trembled for him.
I rose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul went out of me when he spoke. I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer.
The watchmen found me as they went about the city. They struck me, they wounded me; the guards of the walls took my shawl from me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am sick with love.

passages.essence: Half asleep, she hears him knocking and hesitates for a moment; when she opens, he is gone. She searches the night city, is beaten by the watchmen, and is left with only her longing.
reading: Right after the fulfilment of the garden comes the Song’s most painful scene. It begins on the border of sleep: “I was asleep, but my heart was awake.” In Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of mind and will, so she is dozing in body while something in her keeps watch. Many readers take what follows as a dream, which would explain its strange logic: the instant disappearance, the city at night, the violence.

He knocks and pleads, piling up endearments: my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one. His head is drenched with the dew of the night. Her reply sounds almost comic: I have taken off my robe, must I put it on again? I have washed my feet, must I dirty them? It is the reluctance of someone warm in bed, and it lasts only a moment, but the moment is enough.

The middle verses work on two levels at once, and the Hebrew is frank. He puts his hand through “the opening”; her inmost being trembles; she rises and her fingers drip with myrrh on the handles of the bolt. On the surface this is a door with a latch hole. But “hand” is used as a euphemism elsewhere in the Bible, the word for opening means a hole, and myrrh has been the scent of lovemaking throughout the Song. Scholars such as Marvin Pope and J. Cheryl Exum have shown how the scene keeps both meanings in play. The double sense is not a trick; it is how desire actually speaks, through ordinary things.

Then the door opens on emptiness. “My beloved had turned and gone.” The Hebrew is abrupt, two verbs with no connecting word, like a breath caught. “My soul went out of me when he spoke” may look back to his voice at the door, or may mean she almost died of it. She seeks and does not find, calls and gets no answer: the language of the first night search in 3:1–2, but now heavier.

In 3:3 the watchmen simply passed her by. Here they beat her, wound her and strip her shawl. Whatever the guards stand for, the city’s authority, social judgement on a woman alone at night, or simply the cruelty of a nightmare, the scene is shocking in a book so full of delight. Yet her final words are not about her injuries. She turns to the daughters of Jerusalem and asks them to tell him she is “sick with love”, the same phrase she used in 2:5 when she was in his arms. Then it meant fullness; now it means wanting. The Song refuses to let love become a possession. Even after the garden, the beloved can slip away, and desire is renewed by his absence.

words.note: ‘Ēr is the ordinary word for being awake, related to the verb “to awaken” in the refrain of 2:7. The line sets the body’s sleep against the heart’s watch, which made it one of the most quoted verses in Jewish and Christian spirituality. For the poem it creates the half-lit state in which the whole scene unfolds.

A plain word for a hole in a wall or the ground (2 Kings 12:9). Ancient doors could be unbolted from outside by reaching through a hole above the lock, so the line makes literal sense. Its bodily meaning has been recognised by commentators ancient and modern. The rendering “opening” keeps both.

Literally “my innards”, the place where Hebrew locates deep feeling. The verb with it, hāmû, “trembled, churned”, is used of God’s own yearning for Ephraim in Jeremiah 31:20 and Isaiah 63:15. So her response is not shallow excitement but the deepest kind of stirring, the same that scripture ascribes to divine compassion.

A rare word for a light outer wrap, mentioned elsewhere only in the list of fine clothes in Isaiah 3:23. Its loss leaves her exposed and shamed. Some readers connect it with her robe in 5:3: she dressed again to go to him, and the world strips her.

history: The rabbis heard this passage as Israel’s story with God. A famous reading in Song of Songs Rabbah takes “my heart” as God himself: I am asleep, says Israel, careless of the commandments, but the Holy One, the heart of Israel, is awake. The Targum reads the knock as the prophets calling Israel to repent, the hesitation as her refusal, and the beating by the watchmen as conquest and exile.

Christian mystics found here the shape of the spiritual life. Gregory of Nyssa, in his homilies on the Song, praised the sleep in which the senses rest and the mind keeps watch, and he read the beloved’s disappearance as a gift: God withdraws so that the soul will keep reaching further, never resting in what it has already found. Even the watchmen’s blows became for him the wound of love. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote of the Word’s comings and goings in the soul. Most famously, John of the Cross built his poems of the dark night and of the absent Beloved, “Where have you hidden?”, on this scene. Modern readers have seen in it the logic of dream, the vulnerability of women in a hostile city, and the truth that longing and fulfilment cannot be separated.

life.love: A moment’s hesitation, and the beloved is gone. Most relationships are not lost in one great betrayal but in small delays: the call not returned, the door not opened because we were comfortable. What knock have you been slow to answer?
life.body: The scene happens between sleep and waking, when the body knows things before the mind does. Pay attention to what your body registers first: a quickening, a tightening, a reluctance. It is often the earliest and most honest news of what you want.
life.inner: Many traditions describe a season when what we love most seems to withdraw, and seeking only finds silence. The poem does not explain this away. It shows a person who keeps searching and keeps naming her longing aloud. Absence can deepen love rather than end it.

passages.question: When you have hesitated and missed a moment, what did the longing afterwards teach you?

passages.title: This is my beloved

verses.t: What makes your beloved better than any other, most beautiful of women? What makes your beloved better than any other, that you make us swear like this?
My beloved is radiant and ruddy, standing out among ten thousand.
His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting by brimming pools.
His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of fragrant herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping flowing myrrh.
His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels of Tarshish. His body is a panel of ivory, inlaid with lapis.
His legs are pillars of alabaster, set on bases of fine gold. His bearing is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
His mouth is sweetness itself, and all of him is desire. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.

passages.essence: Asked what makes her beloved better than any other, she answers with the Bible’s only full description of a man’s beauty, from head to foot, in gold, ivory, lapis and alabaster. She ends with the simplest words: this is my beloved, and this is my friend.
reading: The daughters of Jerusalem ask a fair question, twice, with a hint of teasing: what is so special about him, that you make us swear oaths on his behalf? Her answer is a poem. Scholars call this form a wasf, an Arabic word for “description”, after the nineteenth century German consul J. G. Wetzstein recorded Syrian village wedding songs that praised the bride and groom part by part. The man has praised her this way in 4:1–7 and will again in 6:4–7 and 7:1–5. This is the woman’s only wasf, and it is unique in the ancient Near East: a woman publicly, joyfully describing the body of the man she loves.

She begins with an overall impression, “radiant and ruddy”, the healthy glow of a young man. The word for ruddy recalls the young David, “ruddy, with beautiful eyes” (1 Samuel 16:12). He “stands out among ten thousand”, as a banner stands out above a crowd. Then she moves from head to foot: a head of the finest gold, hair wavy and black as a raven, eyes like doves at streams of water, cheeks like beds of spices, lips like lilies dripping myrrh.

From the arms downward the images harden into precious materials. His arms are rods of gold set with jewels of Tarshish (perhaps beryl or topaz), his body a panel of ivory inlaid with lapis lazuli, his legs pillars of alabaster on bases of gold. He has become a statue, like the gold and ivory images of gods in ancient temples. Othmar Keel compared this description to Egyptian and Mesopotamian statuary, where such materials signalled divine splendour. The book of Daniel uses the same top-to-bottom pattern for Nebuchadnezzar’s statue with its head of gold (Daniel 2:32). The effect is double. The living images (doves, water, spices, lilies, myrrh) make him sensuous and near; the precious ones make him precious, enduring, almost holy. She sees him as both warm flesh and treasure.

“His bearing is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars”: after the details, she steps back to see the whole man, tall and fragrant like the great forest of the north. Then she comes to his mouth, which she has saved for last: “His mouth is sweetness itself, and all of him is desire.” The kiss she asked for in 1:2 returns.

Her final line moves from beauty to bond: “This is my beloved, and this is my friend.” The Hebrew rē‘î, “friend, companion, neighbour”, is a word of equality and loyalty. After the gold and ivory, the highest thing she can say is that he is her friend. And the poem works. In the next verse the daughters, who began by doubting, ask where he is so they can search for him with her.

words.note: Related to degel, “banner”, which appeared in 2:4 (“his banner over me was love”) and to the bannered hosts of 6:4 and 6:10. The sense is “raised like a standard”, visible above everything else. Among ten thousand, a whole army, he is the one her eyes find at once.

Ṣaḥ means dazzling, clear, bright; ’ādôm is red, the colour of blood and of earth (’ădāmâ). Together they describe glowing, vital skin. Lamentations 4:7 uses the same pair for the nobles of Jerusalem before the famine, “brighter than snow… more ruddy than coral”. It is the look of health and youth.

From the root ḥmd, “to desire”, the same root as the commandment “you shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17). Here the desire is not forbidden but celebrated. The plural form intensifies it: he is not merely desirable, he is “all desires”, desire itself. In Isaiah 64:11 the same word describes the precious things of the Temple.

The common word for friend, companion or neighbour, as in “love your neighbour” (Leviticus 19:18). The man calls her ra‘yātî, “my love, my companion”, many times, but this is the only time she calls him rē‘î. Placed beside “my beloved” at the climax of her poem, it says that their love includes companionship and equality.

history: Jewish tradition read this portrait as a description of God, which made it both treasured and daring. The rabbis applied each feature to the Torah: the Talmud (Eruvin 21b) reads “his locks are wavy”, taltallîm, as tillê tillîm, “heaps upon heaps”, the mounds of teaching that hang on every stroke of every letter. Early Jewish mystical texts called Shi‘ur Qomah, “the measure of the body”, drew on this passage to speak of the immense dimensions of the divine form, a tradition later rabbis treated with great caution.

Christians read it as the beauty of Christ. Medieval interpreters took the golden head as his divinity and the body as his humanity, and the phrase “chief among ten thousand”, as older English Bibles render it, became beloved in Puritan devotion and in hymns that praise Christ as the fairest of all. Modern readers emphasise something the allegories pass over: in a literature where women’s bodies are often described by men, here is a woman who gazes, evaluates and celebrates, and whose praise persuades the other women.

life.love: When asked why she loves him, she does not argue; she describes him with care. Try it: write down, part by part, what you love about someone close to you. The act of attention may change how you see them, and telling them may change them too.
life.body: Her poem joins the living and the precious: doves and gold, spices and ivory. Bodies are both, fragile and soft, and also worthy of the reverence we give to treasure. Notice the beauty of a body you know well, including your own, without first measuring it against an ideal.
life.inner: “This is my friend.” Many contemplatives have said that the highest stage of love, for another person or for God, is friendship: a love that is no longer only longing but companionship. Ask what it would mean to be not only devoted to what you love but its friend.

passages.question: If someone asked you what makes the one you love different from all others, what would you say?

passages.title: Gone down to his garden

verses.t: Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful of women? Which way has your beloved turned, so that we may seek him with you?
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.

passages.essence: The daughters offer to help her search, and she answers with a paradox: he has gone down to his garden, which is where she is. He was never lost. She seals it with the Song’s refrain of mutual belonging: I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.
reading: Her portrait of the man has done its work. The daughters of Jerusalem, who a moment ago asked what was so special about him, now want to find him too: “Where has your beloved gone? Which way has he turned, so that we may seek him with you?” Their question echoes the first night search and the agonised one just before (5:6), and we expect another anxious answer.

Instead she answers calmly, as if she has known all along. “My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.” By now in the Song the garden has a fixed meaning: in 4:12–5:1 the garden is she herself, her body and her love, which she opened to him. So the answer is a riddle with a smile in it. He has not gone anywhere far; he has gone to her. The search that began in 5:6 ends not with a discovery out in the city but with a recognition of where he truly is.

The images of grazing and gathering lilies are tender and sensual. The verb rā‘â means both to pasture a flock and to feed; the man was a shepherd in 1:7 and “grazes among the lilies” in 2:16. Here he is the one who feeds, and the lilies he gathers are the delights of the garden. Many scholars see the scene as another love meeting, described as always in the Song by image rather than statement.

Verse 3 brings the great refrain of mutual belonging. In 2:16 she said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” Now she reverses the order: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” In 7:10 she will say it a third way: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” Readers have long found meaning in the shift. The first form begins with possession, the second begins with self-giving. Love here is not a contract in which each side keeps accounts, but a circle in which belonging and being belonged to cannot be separated.

J. Cheryl Exum notes how often the Song moves between absence and presence without ever settling into one: the lovers seek and find, lose and find again. These three verses are a small model of the whole book. Absence is answered not by a dramatic reunion but by a simple statement of where love lives.

words.note: A question word of direction, “whither”, repeated twice for emphasis. It belongs to the vocabulary of searching that runs through the Song (“tell me where you pasture”, 1:7). The double question makes her answer more striking: she does not say where to look, but where he already is.

The exact flower is uncertain. The word is related to Egyptian sšn, the lotus, and may mean the water lily, a red or white wild lily, or simply bright spring flowers. Keel showed that the lotus symbolised renewal and life in Egyptian art. In the Song lilies mark the places of love: her lips (5:13), her breasts’ pasture (4:5), the beloved’s grazing ground (2:16).

A participle meaning one who pastures or feeds, often used as a noun for a shepherd. The phrase “who grazes among the lilies” is ambiguous: he feeds his flock there, or he himself feeds there. The double sense keeps him both the gentle shepherd of 1:7 and a lover enjoying the garden.

words.gl: I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine
words.note: Four words in Hebrew, built in a perfect mirror: I, to my beloved, my beloved, to me. Their initial letters spell Elul, the name of the Hebrew month before the New Year, which Jewish tradition made a season of return to God. The phrase is often engraved inside wedding rings.

history: For the rabbis, the garden was the place where God dwells among his people. Song of Songs Rabbah identifies “his garden” with the world or with Israel, and the beds of spices and gardens with the synagogues and houses of study, where God goes down to find those who seek him. “To gather lilies” was read in a more sombre way as well: the righteous, whom God gathers to himself at their death, and the verse became a consolation in mourning. The four words of 6:3 gave the month of Elul its devotional meaning, a time when, in a well known Hasidic saying, “the King is in the field”, close and approachable.

Christian readers saw the garden as the Church, into which Christ descends to tend and gather souls, and the mutual belonging as the covenant between Christ and the believer. Teresa of Ávila loved this verse and wrote a poem on “my Beloved is for me and I am for my Beloved”. Modern scholars read it as the lovers’ own vow, and the refrain has become one of the most used verses at weddings, Jewish and Christian alike.

life.love: The friends want to help her search; she realises the beloved is already near. Sometimes we chase connection in the wrong places while it is waiting at home. Look again at the relationships you already have before searching for the one you imagine you are missing.
life.body: “He has gone down to his garden”: presence is physical. Love that lives only in thoughts and messages lacks something the body knows. Find a way today to be with someone in the flesh, simply sharing the same space and time, without needing to achieve anything.
life.inner: “I am my beloved’s” comes first here. Spiritual traditions agree that self-giving, not acquisition, opens the heart. Notice whether you approach what you love, your work, your faith, your people, mainly asking what it gives you, or also asking how you belong to it.

passages.question: Where are you searching far away for something that is already in your own garden?

passages.title: Awesome as bannered hosts

verses.t: You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as bannered hosts.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes coming up from the washing: each one has its twin, and not one of them is missing.
Your cheek behind your veil is like a half of a pomegranate.
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number.
One alone is my dove, my perfect one, the only one of her mother, the bright one of her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her happy; the queens and concubines praised her:
“Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as the bannered hosts?”

passages.essence: He praises her again, but this time her beauty frightens him a little: she is like a city, like an army, like the dawn. Among countless women she is the only one, and even the queens agree.
reading: This is the man’s answer to the search that has run since 5:2. She has found him in his garden (6:2–3), and now he speaks, and the first thing he says is unexpected. She is beautiful as Tirzah and lovely as Jerusalem: he compares her not to a flower or an animal but to two cities, the old royal capital of the northern kingdom and the capital of the south. Cities in the ancient Near East were often pictured as women, crowned with walls and towers. To call her a city is to say she is stately, walled, complete, and not easily taken.

Then comes the strangest phrase: “awesome as bannered hosts”. The word for awesome is used elsewhere of the terror an army or a fearsome people inspires. Love, which so far has been sweetness, wine and spices, here shows another face. Her beauty is not only pleasant; it has authority. That is why he begs her, “Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me.” In 4:9 one glance of her eyes stole his heart. Now he cannot hold her gaze at all. Being truly seen by the one you love can be more than you can bear.

Having said that, he steadies himself in a familiar way: he repeats, almost word for word, lines from his first song of praise (4:1–3). The goats streaming down Gilead, the twin ewes from the washing, the pomegranate cheek behind the veil. The repetition is deliberate. It tells us that after the night of searching, the separation and the beating in the streets (5:6–7), nothing has changed in how he sees her. The praise is the same, as if to say: you are still you, and I am still yours.

Verses 8 and 9 widen the frame. Sixty queens, eighty concubines, young women without number: the numbers rise in a way Hebrew poetry likes, and they evoke Solomon’s famous court. Against this crowd stands a single phrase: “One alone is my dove.” She is the only one, the only one of her mother, the bright one of her who bore her. Love does not compare and choose the best; it simply finds that there is only one. Then a lovely reversal: the very women she might be ranked against see her and call her happy, and the queens praise her.

Their praise is verse 10, and it lifts her into the sky: like the dawn looking down, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun. The words for moon and sun here are the rare poetic ones, lĕbānâ, “the white one”, and ḥammâ, “the hot one”, a pairing used in Isaiah 24:23 and 30:26. The verse ends by returning to its first image, “awesome as the bannered hosts”, which closes the passage like a frame. Many readers hear the hosts of heaven in that last line: the stars, ranked like an army. The woman who once said “do not stare at me because I am dark” (1:6) is now compared to every light in the sky.

words.note: A real city, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel before Omri built Samaria (1 Kings 16:23–24). Its name comes from the root rṣh, “to be pleased with, to delight in”, so the comparison is also a pun: you are as lovely as Lovely Town. Some scholars think its mention points to an early date for this poem; others think it was simply a famous, beautiful name that suited the line.

’Ăyummâ means terrible, dread-inspiring; Habakkuk 1:7 uses it of the Babylonian army. Nidgālôt is a passive form of the root of degel, “banner” (as in 2:4): “those with banners raised”, hence armies. Some scholars connect it instead to an Akkadian verb dagālu, “to look”, giving “awesome as visions” or “as the sights in the sky”. Either way the phrase expresses beauty that commands rather than charms.

From tām, “whole, complete, without flaw”, the word used of Job’s integrity. He called her this already when he knocked at night (5:2). It does not mean flawless in looks so much as whole, undivided, all of a piece. It recalls 4:7, “there is no flaw in you”, and fits the claim that follows: she is one, the only one.

Used twice here: she is the bārâ of her mother (6:9) and “bright as the sun” (6:10). The word means clean, clear, pure, as grain is pure once winnowed, and by extension “choice, favourite”. Translators split between “favourite” and “pure”. This rendering chose “bright” in both places so that the echo between the mother’s favourite and the shining sun can be heard in English.

history: Jewish readers heard in the sixty queens and eighty concubines a picture of the Torah’s abundance. One midrash counts the sixty queens as the sixty tractates of the Mishnah and the eighty concubines as sections of the commentary on Leviticus, with the young women without number as the countless laws: many collections, but “one alone is my dove”, the one people who keeps them. The Targum likewise reads the dove as Israel, faithful among the nations, and the dawn of verse 10 as Israel’s rising after exile.

In the third century Cyprian of Carthage quoted “One is my dove” as proof that there can be only one Church, a use that stayed central to Christian arguments about unity. Medieval writers saw the Church as “terrible as an army with banners”, the Church militant, beautiful and fearsome to evil. Verse 10, “Who is this who looks forth like the dawn?”, entered Catholic liturgy for feasts of the Virgin Mary, especially the Assumption, where Mary is the dawn before Christ the sun. Modern scholars, by contrast, stress the human scene: the lover undone by a gaze, and the old Near Eastern habit of praising a woman as a city and a goddess-like light.

life.love: To love someone is to stop ranking them. He does not say she is the best of sixty queens; he says there is only one. Comparison is how we choose; it is not how we love. If you catch yourself measuring the person beside you against others, notice that the measuring itself is a kind of distance. Notice too that he repeats his old praise after their worst night. Saying the same true thing again, after a hard time, can be the most reassuring thing you do.
life.body: “Turn your eyes away, for they overwhelm me.” Real intimacy can feel too much: a look held a moment longer than usual, being seen without a mask. Many of us look away, joke, or reach for a phone. You do not have to force yourself to bear it all at once. But learning to stay present in that overwhelm, breathing, letting yourself be seen, is part of what makes closeness real rather than pleasant.
life.inner: Beauty here is not soft. It has the force of an army and the height of the dawn. Anything truly beautiful, a person, a piece of music, a landscape, has this double quality: it draws you and it unsettles you, because it asks something of you. The old readers who saw God in this passage were pointing at the same thing: what you most love can also be what you most fear to face directly.

passages.question: Where in my life does something I love also overwhelm me, and do I look away from it or let it look at me?

passages.title: Return, return, Shulammite

verses.t: I went down to the nut garden to look at the new growth of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.
Before I knew it, my desire had set me in the chariots of my people’s prince.
Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, and let us look at you!
Why would you look at the Shulammite, as at the dance of the two camps?

passages.essence: She goes down to an orchard to see if spring has come, and something sweeps her away. Then a chorus calls her back to dance, and she asks why they want to stare at her.
reading: Verse 11 sounds simple: someone goes down to a nut garden to see the new growth, the budding vines, the pomegranates in flower. The words recall 7:12, where she invites him to the vineyards to see the very same things, so this rendering gives the verse to her. Some readers give it to him, continuing his speech from 6:4–10; the Hebrew does not mark the speaker. Either way, the garden is the Song’s favourite place of love (4:12–5:1, 6:2), and to “see whether the vine has budded” is to ask whether the time for love has come.

Verse 12 is the most difficult line in the Song, and possibly one of the most obscure in the whole Bible. Word by word it reads something like: “I did not know, my soul (or my desire) set me, chariots of my people, noble.” Every phrase can be taken more than one way. Is “my soul” the subject (my desire placed me) or the object (I did not know my own soul)? Is ‘ammî-nādîb “my noble people”, or a name, Amminadib? This rendering takes the most common modern view: something happened before she knew it. Her own longing carried her off, as if into a prince’s chariot. Whatever the precise sense, the feeling is clear: a sudden, dizzy transport, love that moves faster than thought.

Then, in 6:13 (7:1 in Hebrew Bibles), new voices cry out four times: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return.” This is the only place she is given a name, or a title. The plural “let us look at you” suggests a group, perhaps the daughters of Jerusalem, perhaps wedding guests. The verb “return” (šûbî) may mean come back, or turn around, as a dancer turns. They want to see her.

Her reply is a question, and it has an edge: “Why would you look at the Shulammite, as at the dance of the two camps?” She does not simply perform. She asks what kind of looking this is. The “dance of the two camps”, or “of Mahanaim”, was evidently something known to the first hearers, a famous dance, perhaps between two lines of dancers, or associated with the town of Mahanaim. We have lost its meaning. What we have is the scene: a woman being looked at, a crowd that wants to watch, and her right to ask why. The next passage (7:1–5), the praise of her body from the feet up, reads naturally as a description of her dancing.

words.note: ’Ĕgôz appears only here in the Bible. It is almost certainly the walnut, a tree brought to the region from Persia; the same word is used for walnut in later Hebrew, and the Persian connection is one reason some scholars date the Song late. Walnuts had erotic associations in the ancient world: in Greek and Roman weddings nuts were thrown, and the split nut was a familiar image of the body.

Nādîb means noble, generous, a prince. Joined to ‘ammî, “my people”, it can be read as “my noble people” or “of a prince of my people”. The Greek translators read a proper name, Aminadab, the name of an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:19–20). Compare 7:1, where she is called bat-nādîb, “daughter of a prince”: the two verses seem to echo each other, whatever they mean.

With the article: “the Shulammite”. Three main explanations: a woman from Shunem (like Abishag the Shunammite, the beautiful young woman of 1 Kings 1:3); a feminine form of Solomon’s name, šĕlōmōh, making her “the Solomoness”, his match; or a word built on šālôm, “the one of peace, the perfect one”. Many scholars think the poet wanted all of these at once. Compare 8:10, where she brings šālôm.

words.gl: the dance of the two camps
words.note: Maḥănāyim means “two camps”. It is also a town east of the Jordan, named when Jacob saw a camp of angels there (Genesis 32:2). The phrase may name a dance associated with the town, or a dance in two rows or two groups facing each other. J. G. Wetzstein, who studied Syrian village weddings in the nineteenth century, described a bride’s sword dance before two lines of guests, and some scholars have seen a parallel.

history: The Targum heard “Return, return” as God’s call to Israel to return from exile to Jerusalem, “so that we may see you”, and read the Shulammite as the people whose name is linked with peace (šālôm). Medieval Jewish commentators wrestled with verse 12 as Christians did; Rashi took it as Israel lamenting its own misdeeds that brought it low, before it was lifted up again. The verse’s obscurity has always invited reading.

Christian readers made Aminadab into a figure. In the Latin Bible the verse reads “my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab”. Some read Aminadab as Christ’s ancestor, and his chariots as the Gospel; others made him an enemy. John of the Cross ended his Spiritual Canticle, his great poem on the soul’s union with God, with the line “and Aminadab did not appear”, meaning the devil no longer had any power to disturb the soul. Modern scholars mostly admit defeat on 6:12 and focus on the scene that is clear: a woman called back to be seen, and her question about the crowd’s gaze.

life.love: Love sometimes arrives like this: you go out to check whether spring has come, and before you know it you are carried away. Being swept off your feet is real, and it is a gift, but notice that the very next verses are about being looked at by others. Falling in love is private; being in love is soon public. It helps to ask, as she does, who is watching and what they want to see.
life.body: “Why would you look at me?” Her question is worth keeping. Being seen and admired can be a pleasure, and the next passage glories in her body. But she does not simply hand herself over to the crowd’s gaze. There is a difference between being seen by someone who loves you and being stared at. It is fine to ask which one is happening, and to dance only for those you choose.
life.inner: Verse 12 resists every translator, and that is its own lesson. Some experiences cannot be pinned down even by those who had them: “before I knew it” is how many people describe a turning point, a conversion, a falling in love. You do not have to fully understand what carried you somewhere in order to know that it did. Some honesty consists in saying: I do not know exactly how I got here.

passages.question: When has my own longing carried me somewhere before I knew it, and what did I do once I noticed?

passages.title: How beautiful your feet

verses.t: How beautiful your feet are in sandals, daughter of a prince! The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the work of a master’s hands.
Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks spiced wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, ringed with lilies.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.
Your neck is like a tower of ivory. Your eyes are the pools in Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus.
Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing hair is like purple: a king is held captive in its tresses.

passages.essence: The fullest praise of her body in the Song, moving from her feet upward as she dances. Each part becomes a jewel, a field, a tower or a pool, until a king is caught in her hair.
reading: This is the third great praise-song of the body in the Song, a form scholars call a wasf, after the Arabic word for “description”. The first two (4:1–7 of her, 5:10–16 of him) moved from the head down. This one begins at the feet and climbs. The likeliest reason is the scene just before it: she has been asked to turn and dance (6:13), and the eye of the watcher rises from the moving feet. Who speaks is not marked. It may be the man, or the onlookers who called “Return, return”; but the closing line, a king held captive, sounds like the lover himself.

She is called “daughter of a prince”, bat-nādîb. Earlier she was a vineyard-keeper burned dark by the sun (1:6). Now her sandalled feet are noble. The curves of her thighs are jewels from a master craftsman; the image is of fine metalwork, smooth and turning. Her navel is a rounded bowl never lacking spiced wine; her belly a heap of wheat ringed with lilies. In a farming culture a heap of threshed wheat was wealth, food for the year, and the rounded shape suggests fertility. Lilies, all through the Song, mark the place of love (2:16, 6:2).

Then the images change scale. Her neck is a tower of ivory; her eyes the pools of Heshbon, a city in Transjordan known for its reservoirs, whose remains archaeologists have found; her nose like the tower of Lebanon looking toward Damascus. To modern ears a nose like a tower is comic. But this poetry does not ask us to picture a literal shape. Each comparison carries a quality: a tower is upright, proud, commanding the view; pools are deep and still and reflect the sky. Her body becomes a map of the whole land, from Heshbon in the east to Lebanon and Damascus in the north and Carmel by the sea.

The last verse brings it home. Her head crowns her like Carmel, the green headland above the Mediterranean, and her hair is like purple, the costly dye made from sea snails and worn by kings. The poet plays on sound: karmel (Carmel) is close to karmîl, crimson. And then the twist that ends the praise: a king is held captive in her tresses. The figure of Solomon, with his queens and chariots, is caught by a few locks of hair. In the Song, royal power repeatedly bows before love.

words.note: Ḥammûqîm occurs only here. It comes from a root meaning “to turn”, the same verb used when he “had turned and gone” in 5:6. So the word suggests curving lines, and perhaps turning movement: the sway of hips in a dance. The poet may be quietly answering that earlier scene: he turned away then; now her turning holds him.

The word is related to šōr, “umbilical cord” (Ezekiel 16:4). Some scholars, notably Marvin Pope, argued that here it refers more intimately to the vulva, since a bowl of wine fits that sense well and the description is moving upward from the thighs. Others keep “navel”. Either way, the image of a bowl that never lacks spiced wine means a source of pleasure that never runs dry.

Carmel is the wooded ridge that runs to the sea above modern Haifa. The name itself means “garden-land, orchard”, from kerem, “vineyard”. So “your head is like Carmel” says: your head is a crowned, green height. It also chimes with karmîl, a rare word for crimson thread (2 Chronicles 2:7), which prepares for the purple of her hair in the next phrase.

Elsewhere this word means water troughs (Genesis 30:38, where Jacob waters his flocks). Here it is used of her hair, perhaps as flowing channels, perhaps as braids. A king “bound in the troughs” is a surprising image: caught where the water runs. Some take it as watering troughs where a flock is held fast; in any case the man of power is the one tied up.

history: The Targum and the rabbis read the dancing woman as Israel at worship. Her beautiful feet in sandals became the feet of Israel going up to Jerusalem three times a year for the pilgrim festivals. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 37a) reads the navel as the Sanhedrin, the high court, which sat at the centre of the world as the navel is at the centre of the body; and it reads “a heap of wheat ringed with lilies” as a lesson in restraint: among people who love the law, even a fence of lilies is enough to keep them from crossing a line.

Christian interpreters, led by the line in Isaiah 52:7 (“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger”), heard in the sandalled feet the preachers of the Gospel, shod to carry good news. The navel and the wheat became the sacraments, the cup and the bread of the Eucharist, a reading found in several medieval commentaries. Modern scholars, beginning with Wetzstein’s observations of Syrian wedding songs, read the passage as a wasf sung for a dancing bride, and Othmar Keel has shown how many of its images, towers, pools and crowns, match the visual language of ancient Near Eastern art.

life.love: Praise that is specific is praise that has looked. He does not say “you are beautiful” and stop; he names the feet, the curves, the eyes, the hair. Most of us praise in generalities, or not at all. Try telling someone you love exactly what you see in them, the particular way they move or laugh. Being seen in detail is one of the deepest ways of being loved.
life.body: The poem moves upward from the feet, and it loves every part along the way, not just the parts our culture tells us to notice. There is no body part here that is shameful or comic to the speaker. If you tend to look at your own body as a list of flaws, try reading this poem slowly, and imagine being described by someone who simply finds you good, from the ground up.
life.inner: A king is caught in her hair: power undone by tenderness. Many traditions say that what is strongest in us gives way not to force but to beauty and love. Think about what in you is most guarded, most like a fortified tower, and what might gently unbind it. The Song suggests that being captured by love is not defeat but a kind of freedom.

passages.question: What would I say if I tried to describe, in detail and without irony, what I find beautiful in the person I love, or in myself?

passages.title: The palm tree

verses.t: How beautiful you are, how pleasant, love, among delights!
This stature of yours is like a palm tree, and your breasts are its clusters.
I said, “I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its branches.” Let your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples,
and your mouth like the best wine
that goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over the lips of sleepers.

passages.essence: Praise turns to resolve: he says he will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruit. In the middle of his sentence she takes over the words, and his wish becomes her answer.
reading: Verse 6 gathers up the whole praise before it: “How beautiful you are, how pleasant, love, among delights!” Here he addresses her as ’ahăbâ, love itself. It is as if the person and the feeling have become one. Some scholars, with support from the Aramaic and other ancient versions, read the consonants slightly differently, giving “daughter of delights”, which would match “daughter of a prince” in 7:1. Either way, the verse is a sigh, the moment where description gives way to desire.

The palm tree is the date palm, tall, straight and slender, with its heavy clusters of fruit at the top. Hebrew has a word for it, tāmār, that was also a woman’s name (Tamar). So her stature is like a palm, and her breasts are its clusters. Then the decision: “I said, I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its branches.” The Hebrew “I said” often means “I thought, I resolved”. Othmar Keel points out that date palms in the ancient world were pollinated by hand: a man climbed the female tree to fertilise its blossoms with pollen from the male. Whether or not the poet had this in mind, the image is of a man climbing toward the fruit.

Then the images multiply, one sense after another: let her breasts be like clusters of the vine (sweetness, wine), the scent of her breath like apples, her mouth like the best wine. The Hebrew word for “breath” here is literally “nose”, ’ap, so the line is about the smell of breath, of being close enough to someone’s face to breathe them in. Apples have appeared before: the man was an apple tree in 2:3, and she asked for apples when sick with love (2:5).

Verse 9 is the turning point. He says, “and your mouth like the best wine”, and she finishes the sentence: “that goes down smoothly for my beloved”. The words “my beloved”, dôdî, are always hers in the Song, so she has taken over in mid-line. It is a beautiful piece of poetic craft: the two voices share one sentence, as two people who know each other well finish each other’s thoughts. The wine he praised in her mouth is the wine she pours for him. The end of the verse is uncertain. The Hebrew reads “gliding over the lips of sleepers”, which may suggest lovers falling asleep together, the wine lingering. The ancient Greek and Syriac versions read “over my lips and teeth”, which is smoother but may be a correction.

words.note: The date palm was a symbol of grace, fertility and uprightness across the ancient Near East; in Mesopotamian and Canaanite art a sacred tree, often a palm, is linked with goddesses of love. Psalm 92:12 says “the righteous will flourish like the palm tree”. Three women in the Bible are named Tamar, and the name itself carries the tree’s beauty.

Found only here. It probably means the stalks or fronds that carry the date clusters at the top of the tree; there is a similar Akkadian word, sissinnu, for the date-palm’s spadix. To “take hold of” them is to reach the fruit itself. The rarity of the word shows the poet using precise, technical vocabulary from date growing.

Another word found only here. It may mean flowing gently, or making to murmur or speak. Some medieval Jewish commentators and the Talmud took it as “making the lips of sleepers speak”, as if the wine, or love, could stir even the sleeping to speech; the rabbis used this to say that the lips of the dead move in the grave when their teaching is repeated.

The standard Hebrew text has “sleepers”, yĕšēnîm. The Greek Septuagint and the Syriac read “lips and teeth”, which would need only small changes to the letters (šinnāyim, “teeth”). Many modern translations follow the Greek. This rendering keeps the Hebrew, because the image of wine lingering on the lips of lovers drifting into sleep fits the scene and the Song’s nights of love.

history: One midrash on Song of Songs reads “This stature of yours is like a palm tree” of the three young men in the book of Daniel (Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah) who stood upright like palms while all the nations bowed to Nebuchadnezzar’s golden image. The Talmud uses “gliding over the lips of sleepers” to teach that when a scholar’s teaching is repeated in his name, his lips move gently in the grave, a lovely idea of how words keep the dead alive.

Christian readers often saw in the palm tree the cross, and in the man climbing it Christ, who “went up” on the cross to gather its fruit, the salvation of the world. The palm was already a symbol of victory and martyrdom (palm branches in John 12:13 and Revelation 7:9). Modern scholars have noticed instead the shared verse 9, where her voice enters his line; Robert Alter and others point to this as one of the clearest signs that the Song is crafted as a dialogue of two equal voices, each answering and completing the other.

life.love: She finishes his sentence. Couples who have been together a long time often do this, sometimes annoyingly. But here it is a sign of deep attunement: his wish and her answer are the same breath. Love grows when we listen closely enough to know where the other is going, and when we let our own words be shaped by theirs. Notice today where your words and someone else’s meet.
life.body: Taste, smell, breath, the sweetness of wine: this passage is all senses at close range. The scent of breath is only noticed when you are near enough to kiss. Much of modern life keeps us at a distance, through screens and at arm’s length. Physical closeness, simply being near enough to breathe someone in, is a language of its own.
life.inner: “I said, I will climb.” Desire becomes decision. There is a moment in any good undertaking when wishing turns into resolve. The ancient readers who saw the cross in the palm tree were thinking of this: the climb toward what you love can be costly. Ask what you long for that is still only a wish, and what climbing toward it would mean.

passages.question: Where is there something I have long admired and wished for, and what would it mean to say, “I will climb”?

passages.title: His desire is for me

verses.t: I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.
Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and spend the night among the henna blossoms.
Let us go early to the vineyards and see whether the vine has budded, whether its blossoms have opened, whether the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.
The mandrakes give out their scent, and over our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have kept for you, my beloved.

passages.essence: She says the words that may be the heart of the Song: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” Then she invites him out of the city into the spring fields, where she will give him her love and everything she has kept for him.
reading: Verse 10 is the third time she says some form of the Song’s great refrain. In 2:16 it was “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” In 6:3 the order turned: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” Now it changes again: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” The claim of possession, “he is mine”, has dropped away. What remains is belonging, and his longing turned toward her. Many readers see in these three versions a growth from possessing to trusting.

The word for desire, tĕšûqâ, occurs only three times in the Bible, and the other two are in the opening chapters of Genesis. After the first disobedience, God tells the woman: “your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). In the Song, the direction is reversed: his desire is for her, and nobody rules anyone. Phyllis Trible, in an influential reading, called the Song “love’s lyrics redeemed”: a return to the garden where man and woman are equals, naked and unashamed. Whether or not the poet meant to answer Genesis, the echo is hard to miss.

Then comes her invitation, the most direct in the Song. “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields.” She takes the lead. They will spend the night among the kĕpārîm, a word that can mean villages or henna bushes (as in 1:14); this rendering chooses henna, because the scene is of open country, vineyards and blossom, not towns. They will rise early to see whether the vine has budded and the pomegranates bloomed: the same words used in 6:11, and the same question the man asked in spring (2:11–13). This time the answer is yes. “There I will give you my love.”

The final verse is full of scent. Mandrakes, plants with a heady smell and fruit thought to increase fertility, give out their fragrance, and over their doors hang choice fruits, new and old, kept for him. The word for mandrakes, dûdā’îm, sounds almost exactly like dōdîm, “love, lovemaking”, which she has just promised. The passage ends with a gift that has been saved: love not as a sudden impulse only, but as something kept, gathered and stored for one person.

words.note: Tĕšûqâ means longing, a yearning that turns toward something. Its only other uses are Genesis 3:16 (the woman’s desire for her husband, under his rule) and Genesis 4:7 (sin’s desire for Cain, which he must master). In both, desire is tangled with power. Here alone it is free and mutual: his desire is for her, and she says so with joy.

The plural of kōper can mean henna, the fragrant shrub whose blossoms she likened to her beloved in 1:14, or villages, the plural of kāpār. Most translations choose “villages”. This rendering chooses henna, because the whole invitation leads away from settled places into fields, vineyards and blossom; but the double sense may be part of the play.

The mandrake has a strong, sweet smell and yellow fruit, and was believed in the ancient world to arouse love and help conception. In Genesis 30:14–16 Rachel buys Reuben’s mandrakes from Leah in exchange for a night with Jacob. The word sounds like dōdîm, “love, lovemaking”, and dôdî, “my beloved”: a pun the poet surely meant, as if the plants themselves were saying the lover’s name.

The fruits she has kept are both fresh and stored from earlier seasons: the whole year’s harvest, everything she has. The phrase suggests a love that has its past and its present, memory as well as novelty. It may also echo the end of 7:9: yĕšānîm, “old”, is spelled like yĕšēnîm, “sleepers”.

history: The Targum reads this passage of Israel going out to the fields to study and pray, and of the righteous whose good deeds are stored up “new and old”: commandments of the scribes and of the Torah, kept for God. The phrase “new as well as old” also recalls Jesus’ saying about the scribe who brings out of his treasure “what is new and what is old” (Matthew 13:52), and Christian commentators from Origen onward often read it as the Old and New Testaments together, both kept for Christ.

Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons on the Song and died before he reached the end of chapter 3, so many medieval commentators took up these later chapters in his spirit, reading the invitation to the fields as the soul’s call to go out from the noise of the city into contemplation. In the modern era, Phyllis Trible’s 1978 reading of 7:10 against Genesis 3:16 made this verse a cornerstone of feminist interpretation: the Song as a recovery of the original, unbroken equality of man and woman.

life.love: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” Notice what she no longer says: that he is hers. Mature love lets go of the need to hold and own, and rests in two things: I belong, and I am wanted. If your love is anxious, try asking whether you are holding on too hard. Sometimes peace comes not from possessing the other but from trusting their longing for you.
life.body: She invites; she takes the lead. In the Song desire is never one-sided and never something done to her. Both speak, both want, both ask. Feeling free to name your own desire, and to invite rather than wait, is part of a healthy intimacy. So is the rest of the passage: the slow walk out to the fields, the early rising, the noticing of buds. Pleasure is not rushed here.
life.inner: “New as well as old.” What you have saved up in a life, old griefs, old joys, long-kept hopes, and what is fresh this season, can all be offered. Many spiritual traditions speak of gathering yourself before giving yourself. Ask what you have been keeping, consciously or not, and for whom; and whether this is the season to bring it out.

passages.question: What have I been keeping, new and old, and for whom am I keeping it?

passages.title: If only you were my brother

verses.t: If only you were like a brother to me, who nursed at my mother’s breasts! If I met you outside, I would kiss you, and no one would think less of me.
I would lead you and bring you into my mother’s house, she who taught me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: why would you stir up, why would you awaken love until it is ready?

passages.essence: She wishes their love could be as open and unremarkable as a sister kissing her brother in the street. Then the old embrace returns, and the warning not to wake love before its time is sounded for the last time.
reading: The wish is a real wish, introduced by the Hebrew idiom mî yittenkā, literally “who will give you?”, the way Hebrew says “if only”. She is not asking for her lover to become her brother. She is asking for the freedom a brother has. In the world of the poem a woman can kiss a sibling in the open and no one looks twice; the same kiss given to a lover would cost her her name. “No one would think less of me” uses the verb bûz, to despise, the very word that will return in 8:7, where the man who tries to buy love is “utterly scorned”. Here she wants a love that no one can scorn because no one even notices it.

The sound of the verse does some of the work. “I would kiss you” is ’eššāqĕkā; in the next verse “I would give you to drink” is ’ašqĕkā. The two words are almost the same, so kissing and giving wine slide into each other, as they have since 1:2, where his love was “better than wine”. The wine is yayin hāreqaḥ, wine mixed with spices, and the “juice of my pomegranates” is something she makes and offers. The pomegranates have been hers all along (4:3, 4:13, 6:7, 7:12). Now she presses them herself.

As in 3:4, she imagines bringing him “into my mother’s house”. The phrase is rare in the Bible. Rebekah runs to her mother’s household (Genesis 24:28) and Naomi tells her daughters-in-law to go back to theirs (Ruth 1:8); both times the setting is a woman’s world, where marriages are talked about and arranged. The words translated “she who taught me” are ambiguous: tĕlammĕdēnî can mean “she will teach me” or “you will teach me”. The old Greek and Syriac versions read something closer to 3:4, “the room of her who conceived me”. Either way, the mother is the quiet presence behind the daughter’s love, the opposite of the angry brothers of 1:6.

Then 8:3 repeats 2:6 word for word: his left hand under her head, his right hand around her. Whatever the wish could not have in public, she has in private. And 8:4 sounds the refrain for the third and last time (2:7, 3:5), but changed. The gazelles and does are gone, and the Hebrew asks mah, “why?”, instead of the usual “do not”. It sounds less like an oath and more like a question to the young women watching: why hurry what cannot be hurried? From here the Song moves to its great statement about what love is.

words.note: A fixed Hebrew way of wishing for what is not so, as when the Israelites in the desert say “if only we had died in Egypt” (Exodus 16:3). It marks the whole verse as longing rather than plan. The idiom tells us the obstacle is real: their love has no public form, and she feels the lack.

words.gl: I would kiss you / I would give you to drink
words.note: From two different roots, nšq (kiss) and šqh (give drink), but almost identical in sound. The pun ties the first line of the Song (“let him kiss me… your love is better than wine”) to its last scenes. Kissing and drinking are one pleasure seen twice.

The usual phrase in the Bible is “father’s house”, the unit of family and inheritance. “Mother’s house” appears only a handful of times, always where women and marriage are in view. Carol Meyers and others have argued it points to a domestic world run by women. In the Song it is the safe, sanctioned place where the lovers can be together.

In 2:7 and 3:5 the refrain says “do not” (’im) and swears by gazelles and does. Here the oath animals vanish and the negative becomes mah, a question. Some read it simply as “do not” in another form; others hear a softer, wiser tone, as if experience has replaced command.

history: Jewish allegory heard the wish for a brother as Israel’s longing for intimacy with God that could be shown openly. The Targum, the old Aramaic paraphrase, reads the passage as the community of Israel speaking in the days of the Messiah: if only he were revealed to us as a brother, we would lead him to the Temple, the “mother’s house”, and there he would teach us to fear the Lord. Rashi follows a similar line, with “she who taught me” as the place where Israel learned Torah.

Christian readers made the brother a figure of the incarnation: Christ became a brother, “nursed at my mother’s breasts”, and so the soul may now kiss him “outside”, without shame. Bernard of Clairvaux and the medieval tradition after him loved this image of a God who could be met openly. Modern readers tend to start from the social setting instead. Michael V. Fox notes that the Egyptian love poems also call the beloved “brother” and “sister” as terms of endearment, which shows how naturally the language of kinship and love mixed in the ancient Near East.

life.love: Most love needs some public form: a name for what you are to each other, a place at the table, a way to be seen together. This passage honours that need without pretending it is small. If your love has to hide, the strain is real. If it does not, notice how much freedom you are standing in, and how often you forget to use it.
life.body: She thinks of a kiss, a cup of spiced wine, fruit she has pressed herself. Desire here is generous and practical; it makes things and offers them. Ask what you can give with your hands, your cooking, your time, rather than only what you want to receive. Pleasure that is made and shared tends to deepen.
life.inner: The changed refrain is the voice of experience. Some things cannot be forced: a feeling, a vocation, a faith, a reconciliation. You can prepare the ground and keep the vineyard, but you cannot command it to bloom. Learning to ask “why hurry?” rather than “why not yet?” is a quiet kind of maturity.

passages.question: Where in my life do I want love to be seen, and where am I content to let it ripen unseen?

passages.title: Love is strong as death

verses.t: Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?
Under the apple tree I woke you. There your mother was in labour with you; there she who bore you was in labour.
Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, passion as relentless as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a very flame of the Lord.
Many waters cannot quench love, and rivers cannot sweep it away. If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.

passages.essence: The heart of the Song. She asks to be worn like a seal on his body, and says what love is: as strong as death, a fire no flood can put out, a thing that cannot be bought.
reading: The passage opens with the question first asked about Solomon’s procession in 3:6: “Who is this coming up from the wilderness?” This time the answer is not a king surrounded by soldiers but a woman “leaning on her beloved”. The verb, mitrappeqet, occurs nowhere else in the Bible; it seems to mean to lean or support oneself. The display of power in chapter 3 has been replaced by two people holding each other up.

Then she speaks. “Under the apple tree I woke you”: the verb is the same ‘wr, “awaken”, that the refrain has used three times (2:7, 3:5, 8:4). Love is to be woken only in its time, and she woke it. The apple tree recalls 2:3, where he was the apple tree and she sat in his shade. Now the tree is the place where his mother was in labour with him, so the lovers’ meeting place is also a place of birth. The Hebrew pronouns here are masculine (“you”, “your mother”), so it is she who speaks to him; some ancient versions and modern scholars alter the vowels to make it his speech, but the received text is coherent as it stands.

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” A seal, ḥôtām, was a carved stone used to sign documents, worn on a cord around the neck or as a ring on the hand (Judah leaves his as a pledge in Genesis 38:18). It was a person’s identity and authority in portable form, kept close to the body. She asks to be that close and that binding: pressed into him as a mark of who he is. Then comes the reason, in four lines of tight parallel. Love (’ahăbâ) is as strong as death; passion (qin’â, ardour, jealousy, fierce commitment) is as relentless as Sheol, the grave. Death and Sheol are the forces that take everyone and give nothing back. Love is their equal: it seizes and does not let go.

Its “flashes” are rĕšāpîm, a word that was also the name of Resheph, a Canaanite god of plague and lightning, here reduced to a word for sparks. The line ends in one of the most debated words in the book, šalhebetyâ. It may be a superlative, “a mighty flame”, since -yâ, short for the divine name, can intensify (as “mountains of God” can mean “very high mountains”). Or it may name God: “a flame of Yah”, the only possible mention of God in the Song. The old Masoretic traditions themselves differed on whether to write it as one word or two. This rendering, “a very flame of the Lord”, tries to keep both senses: a flame so fierce it seems divine.

Verse 7 turns from fire to water. “Many waters”, mayim rabbîm, is the Bible’s phrase for the primeval chaos that God subdues (Psalm 29:3, 93:4), and “rivers” recalls Yamm and Nahar, Sea and River, the enemies of the storm god in the Ugaritic myths. Not even the floods of creation can drown love. The last line drops from myth to the marketplace: a man who offered his whole fortune for love would be laughed at. Love can be given but never bought. That thought leads straight into the brothers and Solomon’s vineyard, where money and control are tested against it.

words.note: Cylinder and stamp seals were carved with a name or image and pressed into clay or wax. They were worn on the body and stood for the owner: Pharaoh gives Joseph his signet as a gift of authority (Genesis 41:42), and God tells Zerubbabel “I will make you like a signet” (Haggai 2:23). To be a seal on someone’s heart is to be their identity, worn where they cannot lose it.

Often “jealousy”, but the word covers any burning, exclusive intensity: zeal for God, rage of a rival, devotion that will not share. God is called “jealous” with the same root (Exodus 20:5). Here it stands parallel to love and means the fierce, possessive side of it, not suspicion but total commitment.

The shadowy place of the dead in the Hebrew Bible, pictured as a mouth that is never full (Proverbs 30:15–16; Isaiah 5:14). Comparing love to Sheol is startling: it is not that love is gentle, but that it is as insatiable and as certain as death.

words.gl: a mighty flame; a flame of Yah
words.note: The ending -yâ is a short form of the divine name. Read as an intensifier it gives “a most intense flame”; read literally, “the flame of the Lord”. The Ben Asher tradition writes it as one word, the Ben Naphtali tradition as two. Whether the Song names God here remains one of its most famous open questions.

history: These verses carried the allegorical readings to their height. In the Talmud (Berakhot 61b), Rabbi Akiva, tortured to death by the Romans, recites the Shema and explains that all his life he had wondered how to love God “with all your soul”, even if he takes your soul; now he could fulfil it. Later Jewish readers linked “love is strong as death” with such martyrdom, and the Targum makes the seal Israel’s plea, in exile, to be set like a seal on God’s heart and never forgotten.

Christian readers heard Christ’s love that went through death, and the soul asking to be marked by him. John of the Cross took the “flame” into the heart of his mystical poetry; his Living Flame of Love describes the Spirit as a fire that wounds and heals. Modern scholarship has made the passage the Song’s summit: one of the very few places where the poet steps back to say what love is. Phyllis Trible read the whole Song as a return to Eden, and here, where love is set against death itself, the reversal is clearest. J. Cheryl Exum sees in it the poem’s deepest wish, that love might be lasting in a world where everything passes.

life.love: To ask to be someone’s seal is to ask to belong, openly and lastingly. It is a vulnerable request, and the Song lets the woman make it plainly. If you love someone, could you say it this directly? And if someone has made you their seal, their identity worn close, do you know the weight of what you carry?
life.body: The seal sits on the heart and the arm: the place of feeling and the place of action. Love that lives only in feeling fades; love that lives only in duty hardens. The body is where the two meet. Small faithful acts, a hand on a shoulder, a ring worn for years, keep love in the body.
life.inner: Strong as death, unquenchable by floods, beyond price: whether or not you believe this flame is divine, these are claims about what lasts. Most of what we chase can be bought or lost. Ask what in your life is neither, and how much of your attention it actually gets.

passages.question: What in my life is as strong as death, and have I set it on my heart?

passages.title: We have a little sister

verses.t: We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?
If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver; but if she is a door, we will board her up with planks of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So in his eyes I have become one who brings peace.

passages.essence: Her brothers talk about their little sister as a problem to be managed. She answers for herself: she is a grown woman, strong as a wall, and has found peace in her lover’s eyes.
reading: The brothers return. We met them in 1:6 as “my mother’s sons”, angry with her, setting her to keep the family vineyards while her own went untended. Here they speak in their own voice, in the plural, about a sister who is “little” and “has no breasts”: not yet of marriageable age. Their worry is “the day she is spoken for”, yĕdubbar-bāh, the day a suitor speaks for her and marriage terms are discussed. In ancient Israel brothers often had a say in such matters (Laban negotiates for Rebekah in Genesis 24). Their concern is protective and also proprietary: her future is theirs to arrange.

Their plan comes as two conditions. “If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver; if she is a door, we will board her up with planks of cedar.” Scholars read this two ways. On one reading the lines contrast: a wall is closed, chaste, and deserves honour (silver ornament); a door opens, so she must be shut in. On the other they are parallel: whatever she turns out to be, the brothers will fortify and adorn her, silver on the wall, cedar on the door, both costly materials. Either way, the brothers see her as a building to be secured.

Verse 10 is her answer, and it takes their own image away from them. “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.” She is not little. She uses their architecture, but now the wall is her own strength and dignity, and the towers recall the man’s praise of her neck as “the tower of David” (4:4) and “a tower of ivory” (7:4). She is not a city waiting for defenders; she is a city that stands.

The final line is a play on names. “So in his eyes I have become one who brings peace”: kĕmôṣ’ēt šālôm, literally “like one finding peace”. Šālôm echoes Šĕlōmōh, Solomon, and Šûlammît, the Shulammite (6:13). “Finding peace” could mean finding favour (as one “finds grace” in someone’s eyes), or contentment; it also echoes the language of a besieged city that “makes peace” by opening its gates (Deuteronomy 20:10–11). This rendering, “one who brings peace”, leans toward the sense that she is both at rest in his gaze and the bearer of peace to him. The brothers wanted to guard her; she has given herself, and found šālôm in the giving.

words.note: Literally “it is spoken in her” or “for her”: the passive of the ordinary verb to speak, used here for a marriage proposal. Compare 1 Samuel 25:39, where David “speaks” for Abigail to take her as wife. The brothers anticipate the negotiation that will decide her life, without asking what she wants.

A city wall keeps out; a door lets in. The pair gives the brothers their two cases, and gives her the image she claims. Her “I am a wall” is not a declaration of refusal (she has plainly given her love) but of integrity: she is whole, of age and her own.

Not just the absence of conflict but completeness, everything in its right place. Its sound runs through the Song in the names Solomon (Šĕlōmōh) and the Shulammite (Šûlammît). Here, just before Solomon’s vineyard, she claims šālôm for herself, quietly taking the king’s name-word as her own.

history: Jewish interpreters read the little sister as a figure of Israel or of a righteous ancestor. Song of Songs Rabbah offers several readings, including one that applies the verse to Abraham, who in his youth “united” the world in the service of God; Rashi reads the passage as the heavenly assembly speaking of Israel in exile, small and without strength, and the wall as Israel’s steadfast faith. The silver battlements become the rewards of faithfulness, and the cedar planks the protection given to the weak.

Christian commentators in the patristic and medieval tradition often saw the little sister as the church of the Gentiles, still young and not yet nourished by full teaching, or as the soul in its first stage of growth. Modern readers have been struck instead by the social drama: a woman talked about by the men of her family who answers back. J. Cheryl Exum and Athalya Brenner, among others, have highlighted how unusual it is in ancient literature for a woman to have the last word on her own body and her own consent, and how carefully the Song gives it to her.

life.love: Families often still speak about a grown child as if she were little. Love that matures includes a moment of saying, kindly and clearly, “I am a wall”: I can stand, I can choose. If you are the brother in this story, notice where protection has become control. If you are the sister, notice where you still wait for permission you no longer need.
life.body: She names her own body without embarrassment and without asking anyone’s approval. There is a peace that comes from being at home in your body: not perfect, but yours. Many people spend years seeing themselves through other people’s worry or judgment. Peace begins when the eyes you are seen by are the eyes of love, including your own.
life.inner: Wall and door are both needed in a life: boundaries that hold, and openings that let love in. The brothers can only imagine one or the other. Maturity is knowing when to stand firm and when to open, and that the decision belongs to the one who will live with it.

passages.question: Where am I still letting others decide whether I am a wall or a door?

passages.title: My vineyard, my own

verses.t: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon. He gave the vineyard to keepers; each was to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.
My vineyard, my very own, is before me. You may have the thousand, Solomon, and the keepers of its fruit two hundred.

passages.essence: A short parable sets Solomon’s profitable vineyard, worked by hired keepers, against her own vineyard, which is hers alone to give. The king can keep his thousand pieces of silver.
reading: After the declaration that love cannot be bought (8:7) and the brothers’ plans to manage their sister (8:8–9), a little parable about property. Solomon owned a vineyard at Baal-hamon. No such place is known, and the name sounds symbolic: ba‘al hāmôn means “lord of a multitude” or “owner of abundance”. He let it out to keepers, each of whom owed him a thousand pieces of silver for the harvest. Isaiah 7:23 speaks of a vineyard of “a thousand vines worth a thousand pieces of silver”, so the figure suggests a large and valuable estate.

Many readers have also heard an echo of Solomon’s famous household: seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, a thousand women in all (1 Kings 11:3). The vineyard, in the Song, is almost always a woman’s body and sexuality: “my own vineyard I have not kept” (1:6). Solomon’s vineyard is love on an industrial scale, owned at a distance and tended by others for profit.

Then she speaks of her own: karmî šellî lĕpānāy, “my vineyard, my very own, is before me”. The phrase “before me” means at my disposal, in my keeping, mine to dispose of. This reverses 1:6, where she complained that her brothers had made her keep everyone’s vineyard but her own. Now she has her vineyard back. She does not need Solomon’s silver, and she is generous about it: “You may have the thousand, Solomon, and the keepers of its fruit two hundred.” Let the king and his hired workers have their profits; what she has cannot be paid for.

Who speaks is debated. Some give these lines to the man, boasting that his one beloved is worth more than Solomon’s estate; the possessive “my vineyard” has been read as his. But the phrase “my vineyard, my very own” so clearly answers her words in 1:6 that most modern readers hear her. On either reading the point is the same: love freely given is worth more than the greatest king’s wealth. This is the last of the Song’s seven mentions of Solomon by name, and he leaves the poem as a figure of what love is not.

words.note: A planted, tended, enclosed vineyard; in the Song a constant image for the woman herself (1:6; compare 2:15, 7:12). Vineyards needed years of care before they gave fruit, and they were a family’s wealth. To call oneself a vineyard is to claim both fruitfulness and value, and here, ownership.

An unknown place name, probably invented for its meaning. Ba‘al means owner or lord (and was also the name of a Canaanite god); hāmôn means crowd, abundance, wealth. The name fits Solomon’s vineyard perfectly: ownership of many, love as mass possession.

Literally “to my face”. In Genesis 13:9 Abram tells Lot “the whole land is before you”, meaning yours to choose. Her vineyard is before her in the same sense: hers to give or keep. After all the talk of brothers, guards and kings, she says plainly that the decision is hers.

history: The rabbis treated “Solomon” in the Song as a name for God, the King “to whom peace belongs” (šĕlōmōh read as “his is the šālôm”). The Talmud (Shevuot 35b) records the view that every Solomon in the Song is holy, a name of God, with one exception: this verse, “the thousand are yours, Solomon”, which refers to the human king. Allegorical readers then took the vineyard as Israel, let out to the nations or to its leaders, and the thousand and two hundred as payment and reward for those who guard it, such as the teachers of Torah.

Christian commentators read the vineyard as the church, entrusted by Christ, the true Solomon, to apostles and pastors, who must render fruit and receive their own reward; the parable of the wicked tenants (Mark 12:1–12) made the connection natural. Modern scholars, Roland Murphy and Michael V.
