Fox among them, read the lines as a contrast between the commercial love of a harem and the personal, free love of the Song, closing the book’s running critique of Solomon’s grandeur.

life.love: The Song refuses to treat love as a transaction. Notice where relationships around you run on Solomon’s terms: keepers, quotas, returns. Love that keeps accounts can work for a while. Love that says “my vineyard is mine to give” is freer, and it can be generous with everyone else’s accounts too.
life.body: To say “my vineyard is before me” is to say my body is mine, to give or keep. Consent is not a modern idea added to the Song; it is in the Song’s bones. If your sense of your body has been shaped by what others expected of it, these lines are an invitation to take it back into your own care.
life.inner: Solomon has everything and tends nothing himself. There is a spiritual lesson there for anyone with a lot to manage: what you only own, you do not know. Ask which vineyard in your life you have handed to keepers, and which you tend with your own hands.

passages.question: What do I own that I do not tend, and what do I tend that is truly mine to give?

passages.title: Make haste, my beloved

verses.t: You who sit in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice: let me hear it.
Run away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.

passages.essence: The Song does not end with a wedding or a death but with an invitation and a parting. He asks to hear her voice; she answers by sending him off, swift as a gazelle, to the mountains of spices.
reading: The last two verses are short and slightly mysterious. He speaks to her as hayyôšebet baggannîm, “you who sit (or dwell) in the gardens”. The form is feminine, so she is the one in the gardens: the garden that was her own body in 4:12–5:1 has become the place where she lives. “Companions” (ḥăbērîm) are listening for her voice, the same word as in 1:7, where she worried about wandering among his companions’ flocks. Now his companions are the ones waiting on her. “Let me hear it” echoes 2:14, “let me hear your voice”, when she was hidden in the clefts of the rock. He asked then and asks still.

She answers, and her answer is the last line of the book: “Run away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.” The verb bĕraḥ normally means to flee or run off. That is surprising at the end of a love poem. Some take it as a lovers’ tease, “off you go”, or as a wish for him to hurry, “make haste” as older translations have it. Many readers hear in it the rhythm that runs through the whole Song: presence and absence, finding and losing, approach and withdrawal.

The line deliberately echoes 2:17: “turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the cleft mountains.” But the mountains have changed. In chapter 2 they were “cleft mountains”, hārê bāter, mountains of separation; here they are hārê bĕśāmîm, mountains of spices. Spices, bĕśāmîm, have run through the Song as the scent of her body and her garden (4:10, 4:14, 4:16, 5:1, 6:2). So the gazelle she sends away is bounding over her own hills. The farewell may also be a summons.

So the Song ends open. There is no ceremony, no resolution, no final union described. The woman spoke the first words of the poem (“let him kiss me”, 1:2) and she speaks the last. Love here is not a story that concludes but a movement that keeps going, desire renewed by distance. That is true to the poem’s whole shape: the search, the finding, the losing, the search again. The book leaves its lovers mid-run.

words.gl: you who dwell in the gardens
words.note: A feminine participle: she is addressed as the one who lives among gardens. The plural “gardens” widens the private garden of 4:12 into a whole landscape. In Jewish tradition the phrase was applied to Israel dwelling among the nations, or to students sitting in houses of study.

The ordinary verb for fleeing, used of Jacob running from Laban (Genesis 31:21) and Moses fleeing Pharaoh (Exodus 2:15). Its ending of the Song is deliberately open: it can sound like sending him away, urging him to hurry, or inviting him onward to her “mountains of spices”. Translators choose; the Hebrew holds all three.

The last image in the book. It answers “the cleft mountains” of 2:17 and “the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense” of 4:6, his words about her body. Bĕśāmîm, spices or balsam, are the Song’s signature scent. The landscape of the beloved has become a landscape of fragrance.

history: Jewish allegory read the ending as Israel’s prayer in exile. Rashi takes “flee, my beloved” as a plea to God to flee from this exile and redeem his people, and the mountains of spices as Mount Moriah, the site of the Temple, where the incense rose. The Targum likewise has the elders of Israel pray that in their distress God will be swift as a gazelle to hear them. The book ends, on this reading, not in fulfilment but in hope, like Jewish prayer itself.

Christian readers heard the church’s longing for Christ’s return, the same cry as the last words of the New Testament: “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). Gregory of Nyssa saw the whole Song as the soul’s endless ascent, never finally arriving because God is infinite, and an open ending suits that vision. Modern readers, including Ariel and Chana Bloch and J. Cheryl Exum, note that the woman has the first and last word, and that the poem preserves desire by refusing to close it.

life.love: Long love includes leaving and returning: work, travel, separate interests, nights apart. The Song does not treat absence as failure. It treats it as part of the rhythm that keeps desire alive. Can you send someone you love off with a blessing, trusting that the mountains they run over are, in some sense, still yours?
life.body: The last image is a body in motion, swift and alive, over hills full of scent. The Song ends not at rest but running. Let your sense of love and desire include energy, play, chase. Stillness has its place in the poem, but so does the gazelle.
life.inner: Many spiritual traditions say the longing itself is a form of presence: to want God, or truth, or love, is already to be turned toward it. The Song closes on longing, not possession. If your inner life feels unfinished, that may be its true shape, not its flaw.

passages.question: Can I let what I love stay free, trusting that longing is part of loving?

themes.name: The garden
essay: The garden is the Song’s central image for the woman herself, and for love as a place. At 4:12 he calls her “a garden locked, a spring locked, a fountain sealed”: private, precious, not open to anyone. At once the garden fills with every spice and fruit, and with water flowing down from Lebanon. Then she answers him and changes its owner: “my garden” becomes “his garden” (4:16), and he comes into it (5:1). What was locked is opened, not taken, by her own invitation.

Gardens in the ancient Near East were luxuries of kings, walled oases of shade, water and fruit; the word pardēs at 4:13 is the Persian word that gives us “paradise”. Readers since Phyllis Trible have heard an echo of Eden: there a garden was lost and desire became tangled with blame; here a garden is found again and desire is mutual and good. Jewish allegory heard the garden as Israel, kept faithful among the nations; Christian readers heard the Church, or the soul enclosed and fruitful, and the sealed fountain became an image of Mary.

Later the man “has gone down to his garden” (6:2) and she to “the nut garden” (6:11), and the Song ends with her as one “who sits in the gardens” (8:13). The garden is where love lives when it is allowed to grow.

themes.name: The vineyard
essay: Vineyards in the Song are both real places of work and an image of the woman’s body and sexuality. The double meaning arrives in her first speech: her brothers made her keep the vineyards, “my own vineyard I have not kept” (1:6). She has been working in the sun for others, and has not tended herself; she has not been guarded, perhaps, in the way her brothers would like.

The image returns throughout. The little foxes that ruin the vineyards in blossom (2:15) are whatever threatens young love. In spring she and he go out to see whether the vine has budded (6:11, 7:12), and “there I will give you my love”. In the last chapter she sets her own vineyard against Solomon’s: his is vast, let out to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver, but “my vineyard, my very own, is before me” (8:12). The woman who could not keep her vineyard at the start disposes of it freely at the end.

For Israel’s prophets the vineyard was a familiar image of God’s people (Isaiah 5:1–7), and Jewish and Christian allegory naturally read the Song’s vineyards in that light. Read plainly, the vineyard says that love is something cultivated over seasons, fragile in blossom, and ultimately one’s own to give.

themes.name: The gazelle and the young stag
essay: The gazelle is the Song’s animal of love: swift, graceful, shy, and wild. The man comes “like a gazelle or a young stag”, leaping over the mountains (2:9). Her breasts are “two fawns, twins of a gazelle” (4:5, 7:3). When she makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear not to awaken love, they swear “by the gazelles and by the does of the field” (2:7, 3:5).

That oath is a piece of wordplay. The usual oath would be “by the Lord of hosts” or “by God Almighty”, ’ĕlōhê ṣĕbā’ôt and ’ēl šadday. The Hebrew for “by the gazelles” and “by the does of the field”, biṣbā’ôt ’ô bĕ’aylôt haśśādeh, sounds remarkably like those divine names. The Song swears by the creatures of love, and in doing so avoids the name of God while still faintly echoing it. In the art of the ancient Near East, as Othmar Keel showed, gazelles were associated with the goddess of love, which fits.

The gazelle also frames the poem. At 2:17 she sends him away to be a gazelle on the cleft mountains until morning, and the Song’s very last words are the same: “be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices” (8:14). Love here does not end in possession. It ends, as it began, in motion.

themes.name: Wine
essay: Wine is the Song’s measure of pleasure. The first thing the woman says of her lover’s love is that it is “better than wine” (1:2, 1:4), and he says the same of hers (4:10). Love is the thing that outdoes the best thing people know: wine was joy, festivity and abundance in the ancient world.

Wine is also a place and a state. He brings her to “the house of wine” (2:4), the banqueting hall or simply a place of celebration; he drinks “my wine with my milk” in the garden (5:1), and someone calls to the lovers, “Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love.” Her mouth is “like the best wine” (7:9), her navel “a rounded bowl that never lacks spiced wine” (7:2), and she would give him “spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates” (8:2). Taste and intoxication run together with kissing and lovemaking; the Song does not separate the pleasures of the body.

Allegorical readers took the wine in many directions: the words of the Torah, sweeter than any wine; the wine of the Eucharist; the “sober intoxication” of mystics drunk on God. Bernard of Clairvaux and John of the Cross both wrote of the inner wine cellar of the soul. The plain sense is simpler and deeper: love is the best of what life tastes like.

themes.name: Spices and perfume
essay: No book of the Bible smells as much as the Song. Nard, myrrh, henna, frankincense, saffron, sweet cane, cinnamon, aloes: many of these were precious imports from Arabia, India and beyond, the luxuries of kings and temples. In the Song they belong to lovers. Her nard gives out its fragrance while the king is on his couch (1:12); he is a sachet of myrrh between her breasts (1:13); his name is “oil poured out” (1:3).

The catalogue reaches its height in the garden of 4:12–5:1, where she is an orchard of every spice, and in her wish that the winds blow on her garden “and let its spices flow” (4:16). His cheeks are “beds of spices” (5:13), his lips drip myrrh; when she rises to open to him at night, her own fingers drip with myrrh on the bolt (5:5). The Song ends on “the mountains of spices” (8:14), which may be the woman herself.

Scent works in the Song as presence at a distance: it arrives before the lover does and lingers after he is gone. In the Bible, the same spices were used for the holy anointing oil and the incense of the sanctuary (Exodus 30), which gave allegorical readers an easy bridge from love to worship. Myrrh was also used for burial, a quiet reminder that the Song’s love is strong as death.

themes.name: The dove
essay: The dove is one of his favourite names for her. Her eyes are doves (1:15, 4:1); she is “my dove, in the clefts of the rock” (2:14), hidden and shy; when he knocks at night she is “my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one” (5:2); she is the one dove among sixty queens (6:9). Once she uses the image for him: his eyes are “like doves beside streams of water” (5:12).

What do doves suggest? Gentleness, softness, the soft repeated voice; perhaps the soft grey or the quick movement of eyes; faithfulness, since doves pair. In ancient Near Eastern art, as Othmar Keel argued, doves were messengers of love and birds of the love goddess, and eyes like doves are eyes that send love. The turtledove whose voice is heard in spring (2:12) adds the sense of the season of mating.

Jewish interpreters loved the dove as an image of Israel: faithful, hunted, hiding in the clefts of the rock at the Red Sea when Pharaoh pursued. Christian readers connected it with the dove of the Holy Spirit at Jesus’s baptism, and with the soul’s simplicity. The Song itself keeps the image close and tender: the dove is the beloved as someone hidden whom the lover longs to see and hear.

themes.name: The search by night
essay: Twice the woman goes out into the city at night to look for the one her soul loves. The two scenes are built alike: she is in bed, he is absent, she seeks him and does not find him, the watchmen who go about the city find her. But they end differently. In the first (3:1–5), she finds him just after passing the watchmen, holds him, and will not let go until she has brought him to her mother’s house. In the second (5:2–8), he knocks, she hesitates, opens too late, and he is gone; the watchmen beat her and take her shawl, and she can only beg the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick with love.

Some scholars read these as dreams, especially the second, which begins “I was asleep, but my heart was awake”. Either way, they give the Song its shadow: love is not only fulfilment but absence, missed moments, and the vulnerability of a woman who goes out alone at night for love. The violence of 5:7 is real, and readers such as J. Cheryl Exum have asked what it says about the risks the woman takes.

For the mystics the night search became one of the great images of the spiritual life: the soul seeking God, who withdraws in order to be sought more deeply. John of the Cross’s “dark night” and the opening of his Spiritual Canticle, “Where have you hidden, Beloved?”, grow from these verses.

themes.name: Do not awaken love
essay: Three times the woman makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear an oath: “do not stir up, do not awaken love until it is ready” (2:7, 3:5, 8:4). The first two times the oath is by the gazelles and the does of the field; the third time the oath is shortened and turned into a question, “why would you stir up…?” Each time, it comes just after a moment of intimacy: the embrace, the finding of the beloved, the embrace again. It works as a refrain that closes a section.

Its meaning is debated. The Hebrew could mean: do not disturb our lovemaking until it is finished; or do not arouse love in yourselves before the time is right. The word translated “until it is ready” is literally “until it pleases”, as if love had a will of its own. Many readers take it as a piece of hard-won wisdom from a woman who knows how overwhelming love is: do not force it, do not hurry it, do not play with it. She has felt love as sickness (2:5, 5:8); she knows its power.

Jewish tradition sometimes read the oath as a warning not to force the redemption before God’s time. Read plainly, it remains one of the wisest sayings about love anywhere: love has its own timing, and a wise person respects it.

themes.name: My beloved is mine
essay: Three times the woman states the heart of the Song in a few words. At 2:16: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” At 6:3, reversed: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” At 7:10, transformed: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.” The Hebrew is short and musical, and it is among the most quoted lines of the Bible: in its reversed form, ’ănî lĕdôdî wĕdôdî lî, it is engraved on countless wedding rings.

The order matters. In the first she begins with possession, “he is mine”; in the second she begins with giving, “I am his”; in the third possession has fallen away and been replaced by his desire for her. Phyllis Trible pointed to the word for desire, tĕšûqâ, which occurs elsewhere only in Genesis 3:16 (and 4:7): there the woman is told “your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.” In the Song the direction is reversed, and no one rules.

The refrain describes a love without hierarchy: two people who belong to each other freely and equally. Religious readers have heard in it the covenant formula, “I will be your God and you shall be my people”, and the mutual love of God and the soul. Either way, its point is reciprocity.

themes.name: The mother’s house
essay: Fathers never appear in the Song. Mothers do, again and again. When the woman finds her lover she brings him into “my mother’s house, into the room of the one who conceived me” (3:4), and she longs to do it again (8:2): “she who taught me.” Her mother’s sons are her brothers (1:6). He is crowned by his mother on his wedding day (3:11). She is “the only one of her mother” (6:9). He was born under the apple tree where she now wakes him (8:5).

Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the household is called “the father’s house”, and marriages are arranged between fathers. The “mother’s house” is rare: Carol Meyers noted that it appears in contexts about women, love and marriage, such as Rebekah running to her mother’s household in Genesis 24:28 and Naomi sending her daughters-in-law home to their mothers in Ruth 1:8. In the Song it is the woman’s safe place and the place where love is passed from one generation to the next.
The theme gives the Song a sense of lineage and continuity. Love is not only something that happens between two people; it has come down through mothers, and it will go on.

themes.name: Lebanon and the far places
essay: Lebanon is the Song’s land of height, wildness and splendour. Its mountains carried snow (the name means “white”) and forests of cedar, the most prized timber of the ancient world. Solomon’s carriage is made of its wood (3:9); the scent of her clothes is “like the scent of Lebanon” (4:11); streams flow down from Lebanon into her garden (4:15); he looks “like Lebanon, choice as the cedars” (5:15); even her nose is like “the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus” (7:4).

At 4:8 he calls her to come with him from Lebanon, from the peaks of Amana, Senir and Hermon, “from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards”. These are real mountains in the far north, but here they are a mythic landscape: the bride as someone remote, wild, guarded by dangerous creatures, who must come down to him. The Song’s map is full of such places, each with a feeling: En-gedi’s oasis, the black tents of Kedar, the hills of Gilead, the pools of Heshbon, Carmel’s height, the beauty of Tirzah and Jerusalem.
Together they make the lovers larger than life. Each is a whole country to the other, full of wonders and distances.

themes.name: Solomon and the king
essay: Solomon’s name appears seven times in the Song, and “the king” several more. The title gives the Song to him. The woman says “the king has brought me into his rooms” (1:4) and “while the king was on his couch” (1:12). A grand procession brings “Solomon’s couch” up from the wilderness, surrounded by warriors, and the daughters of Zion are called to see him crowned on his wedding day (3:6–11). At 7:5 a king is held captive in her hair.

Who is this king? In the old drama theories, a real Solomon. In the reading of most scholars today, “king” is a lover’s word: as in the Syrian village weddings described by Wetzstein, where the groom and bride were honoured as king and queen, the beloved becomes royal in the eyes of love. The woman may simply be calling her shepherd lover “the king”, as he calls her “daughter of a prince” (7:1).

But Solomon also stands for wealth, power and a harem of “sixty queens and eighty concubines” (6:8; 1 Kings 11 gives him a thousand). And at the very end the woman sets her single vineyard against all his (8:11–12): keep your thousand pieces of silver, Solomon. Next to love, the glory of the greatest king is beside the point.

themes.name: The daughters of Jerusalem
essay: The daughters of Jerusalem are the Song’s chorus: a group of city women to whom the woman speaks, confides, and makes swear. She tells them she is dark and lovely (1:5); she makes them swear three times not to awaken love (2:7, 3:5, 8:4); she sends them to tell her lover she is sick with love (5:8). They answer her with questions that let her sing: “What makes your beloved better than any other?” (5:9) and “Where has your beloved gone?” (6:1). Once they are called “daughters of Zion” and invited to look at King Solomon (3:11).

They serve several purposes in the poem. They give the woman an audience, so her love becomes something shared and spoken, not only private. They represent the city, its polish and its gaze, set against her country life and sunburnt skin (1:6). And they are, perhaps, the young women who have not yet loved, to whom she passes on what she has learned: do not hurry love.
Allegorical readers made them the nations of the world, or souls not yet perfected. For the modern reader they are simply us, the listeners, invited to ask what love is and to hear her answer.

themes.name: Love strong as death
essay: Near the end the Song steps back from its scenes and says what love is. “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, passion as relentless as the grave” (8:6). A seal was a person’s signature, worn on a cord over the heart or as a ring; it was identity and authority. She asks to be his identity, worn against his skin.

Then come the great comparisons. Love is as strong as death, the one power no one escapes; passion is as relentless, or as fierce, as Sheol, the grave that never gives up what it takes. Its flashes are flashes of fire, “a very flame of the Lord” (šalhebetyâ), perhaps the only place God is named in the Song, perhaps simply “a mighty flame”. Many waters, the ancient image of chaos and death, cannot quench it, and rivers cannot sweep it away (8:7). And love cannot be bought: whoever offers all his wealth for it would be scorned.

These verses are the Song’s summit and its most quoted words. They make no promise that love defeats death; they say that love is death’s equal, a force of the same order. Wherever human beings have faced loss with love, these lines have been read.

themes.name: The apple tree
essay: The tappûaḥ was probably the apple, though some scholars suggest the apricot or quince. Whatever the fruit, it is sweet and fragrant. At 2:3 the woman says her beloved is like an apple tree among the trees of the forest: among ordinary trees, the one that gives shade and fruit. “In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.” The image is quietly sensual, and the next verses make it plain.

She asks to be refreshed with apples, for she is sick with love (2:5); he wants the scent of her breath to be like apples (7:8). Then, near the end, the apple tree returns with a new meaning: “Under the apple tree I woke you. There your mother was in labour with you” (8:5). The place of love is also the place of birth. The tree joins the lovers to the generations before them and, by implication, after them.

Christian readers made much of the apple tree as Christ, under whose shadow the soul rests, a reading carried into English in the hymn “Jesus Christ the Apple Tree”. The popular link between the apple and Eden is later and not in Genesis, but it gave the Song’s apple tree an added resonance: here, the fruit is sweet and nothing is forbidden.

themes.name: Lilies
essay: The šôšannâ was probably not the tall white lily of later art but a common wildflower; scholars have proposed the lotus (a favourite of Egyptian love poetry), the anemone or the crocus. The name lives on in the name Susanna. She calls herself “a lily of the valleys” (2:1), modestly, an ordinary wildflower; he turns her words into praise: “Like a lily among thorns is my love among the young women” (2:2).

Lilies then become the setting of love. He “grazes among the lilies” (2:16, 6:3), a phrase that is gentle and frankly suggestive at once: he feeds where she is. Her breasts are fawns grazing among the lilies (4:5); his lips are lilies, dripping myrrh (5:13), which suggests red rather than white flowers; her belly is “a heap of wheat, ringed with lilies” (7:2); he goes down to his garden to gather lilies (6:2).

The lily gave its name to the Christian image of Mary and to many hymns, and to the Jewish reading of Israel as a lily among thorns, keeping faith among the nations. In the Song itself it is the flower of the beloved, small and common, lovely beyond its size.

intro.title: The Song in brief
p: The Song of Songs is a short book of love poetry, eight chapters and 117 verses, in which a woman and a man speak to each other and about each other with open delight. They praise each other’s bodies, long for each other when apart, search for each other through a city at night, and meet in gardens, vineyards and fields that seem to burst into flower around them. There is no plot to speak of, no moral, no lesson stated. There is desire, absence, finding, and praise.

Its Hebrew title, šîr haššîrîm, “the song of songs”, is the Hebrew way of making a superlative, like “holy of holies” or “king of kings”: the finest of all songs. Readers through the centuries have agreed. It is quoted at weddings and funerals, set to music by Palestrina and Monteverdi, and woven into the prayers of Jewish and Christian mystics. It has given the world some of its most lasting lines about love: that it is strong as death, that many waters cannot quench it, that it should not be woken before it is ready.

What makes the Song remarkable is where it sits. It is in the Bible, yet it never mentions God, except perhaps in a single compressed word at 8:6. It does not mention covenant, law, prayer, sacrifice or Israel’s history. It says nothing about marriage in the legal sense, and nothing about children. Its centre is the experience of two lovers, and its point of view is, unusually for ancient literature, mostly the woman’s. That is why it has been both cherished and argued over: for two thousand years readers have asked what a love song is doing in scripture, and their answers make up one of the richest stories in the history of reading.

One answer, the one most scholars now give, is simple. The Song is in the Bible because human love belongs there: desire, beauty, longing and faithfulness are part of the good creation, and a sacred library would be poorer without a book that says so. Another answer, the one that kept the Song alive for most of its history, is that it is an allegory: the love between God and Israel, or Christ and the Church, or God and the soul, told in the language of the most intense love people know. You do not have to choose before you begin. The commentary in this app reads the poem first as what it plainly is, and then shows how each passage has been heard by those who read it as a song about God.

intro.title: Title, author and date
p: The first verse reads “The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s.” The Hebrew lišlōmōh can mean “by Solomon”, “for Solomon”, “about Solomon” or “in the manner of Solomon”, and the same ambiguity hangs over the psalm titles “of David”. Solomon was remembered as a poet (1 Kings 4:32 credits him with 1,005 songs) and as a lover of many women, so his name was a natural one to attach to the finest love song. He also appears inside the poem, at 3:6–11 and 8:11–12, but always in the third person, and at 8:12 the woman dismisses his wealth in favour of her own vineyard. Very few scholars today think he wrote it.

The language points later than Solomon’s tenth century BCE. The Song uses the short relative particle še- (“which, that”) throughout, rather than the classical ’ăšer; tellingly, ’ăšer appears only in the title, which was probably added by an editor. It uses pardēs for “orchard” at 4:13, a loan from Old Persian (the source of our “paradise”), and ’appiryôn for “carriage” at 3:9, which may come from Persian or from Greek phoreion. There are Aramaic forms, such as bĕrôtîm for “cypress” at 1:17 and nāṭar for “keep” at 1:6. Features like these are typical of Hebrew from the Persian period (sixth to fourth centuries BCE) or later.

Some evidence pulls the other way. At 6:4 the woman is compared to Tirzah, a city that was the capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria was built in the ninth century, and some scholars take this as a sign of early material. Others answer that a poet can use an old name for its sound and its memory (Tirzah means something like “she is pleasing”). Some of the Song’s features may also reflect a northern dialect rather than a late date. Proposals therefore range from the reign of Solomon to the Hellenistic third century BCE. The most common view is that the Song took its final form in the Persian or early Hellenistic period, possibly drawing on older songs and a long tradition of love poetry. What can be said for certain is that it was accepted as scripture by the first century CE, and that it belongs to a world in which love poems were a living, popular art.

intro.title: Who is speaking
p: The Hebrew text has no stage directions and no speaker names. But Hebrew grammar marks gender far more than English does: verbs, pronouns and even “you” have masculine and feminine forms. When a line says “you are beautiful” with a feminine “you”, the speaker is addressing a woman; when the verbs are feminine plural, a group of women is being addressed. This lets readers follow the conversation with some confidence most of the time, and it reveals something striking. The woman speaks more than anyone else, well over half of the poem. She opens the Song and she closes it. She initiates, invites, searches, and describes her lover’s body as frankly as he describes hers. Very few texts from the ancient world give a woman’s desire such a voice.

Other voices come and go. The “daughters of Jerusalem” are a group of city women whom she addresses, swears to secrecy, and who answer her questions (5:9, 6:1); they act something like a chorus. Her “mother’s sons”, the brothers, are angry with her at 1:6 and speak protectively, perhaps too protectively, at 8:8–9. Some lines, such as the procession of Solomon at 3:6–11 or the call “Eat, friends, drink” at 5:1, seem to come from a narrator or a crowd. In several places the speaker is genuinely uncertain, and good scholars disagree.

Because the speakers alternate, many readers since the early church have treated the Song as a drama. In the nineteenth century two versions were popular. In the two-character reading, defended by Franz Delitzsch, Solomon falls in love with a country girl, the Shulammite, and marries her. In the “shepherd hypothesis” developed by Heinrich Ewald and others, there are three characters: Solomon tries to win the Shulammite to his harem, but she stays faithful to her shepherd lover back home. Both readings require supplying a great deal that the text does not say, and most scholars have abandoned them.

The real question today is whether the Song is one poem or an anthology. Some, like Marvin Pope and many earlier critics, saw a collection of separate love songs, perhaps twenty or thirty, gathered under one title. Others, like J. Cheryl Exum and Roland Murphy, stress how the refrains, repeated images and returning scenes bind it together, so that even if it was assembled from smaller pieces it reads as one work with two consistent lovers. This app follows that second instinct while keeping the joins visible. Note that the speaker labels (She, He, Friends, Brothers, and a narrating voice) are interpretation, not part of the text. They follow the grammar where it is clear, and the majority of scholars where it is not; the commentary flags the disputed places.

intro.title: How it has been read
p: The earliest debate we know of took place among the rabbis. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5, compiled around 200 CE) records a discussion about whether the Song “makes the hands unclean”, the rabbinic way of asking whether a book is holy scripture. Rabbi Akiva answers with famous force: no one in Israel ever disputed it, for the whole world is not worth the day on which the Song of Songs was given to Israel; all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. Another early saying, attributed to him in the Tosefta, condemns anyone who sings it like a common song at a banquet. Together they show two things: that the Song was being sung as a love song, and that its defenders heard something much more in it.

That something was the love between God and Israel. The Aramaic Targum of the Song, probably from the early medieval period, retells it verse by verse as the history of Israel, from the Exodus and Sinai through the Temple, exile and return, to the coming of the Messiah. The midrash Song of Songs Rabbah gathers centuries of rabbinic interpretation in which the kisses of 1:2 are the words of the Torah given at Sinai. Rashi (1040–1105), whose commentary became standard in Jewish study, read it as the voice of Israel in exile, like a widow remembering the love of her youth and longing for her husband’s return. Abraham ibn Ezra offered a literal reading alongside the allegorical one. In the Kabbalah, the lovers became aspects of the divine life itself, and Jewish mystics in Safed began welcoming the Sabbath as a bride with lines from the Song. To this day it is read in synagogue at Passover, the festival of spring and of Israel’s first love in the wilderness.

Christian readers took up the same method with a new pair of lovers. Hippolytus of Rome, early in the third century, wrote the first Christian commentary we know of. Origen of Alexandria (died about 254) set the pattern for a thousand years: the bride is the Church, and also each individual soul, and the bridegroom is the Word of God. He warned that only the spiritually mature should read the book. Gregory of Nyssa preached fifteen homilies on it as a ladder of endless ascent into God. Bernard of Clairvaux, in the twelfth century, preached eighty-six sermons on the Song and only reached the beginning of chapter 3. In sixteenth-century Spain, John of the Cross, imprisoned in a cell in Toledo, composed the Spiritual Canticle, a love poem deeply shaped by the Song, and Teresa of Ávila wrote meditations on its opening verses. For these readers the erotic language was not embarrassing; it was the only language strong enough for union with God.

There were always dissenters. Theodore of Mopsuestia (died 428) read the Song as Solomon’s love poetry, connected with his marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter. His views were condemned after his death, and the literal reading went underground for centuries, though it never quite disappeared. The modern turn came in the nineteenth century. J. G. Wetzstein, a Prussian consul in Damascus, described Syrian village weddings in which the couple were honoured as “king” and “queen” for a week and songs praising the bride’s body were sung; he called them by their Arabic name, waṣf, and many scholars saw the Song in that light. Others, notably Theophile Meek in the 1920s, argued that the Song began as liturgy for a Mesopotamian “sacred marriage” between a god and goddess; that theory is now largely abandoned. The most fruitful comparison came with the publication of Egyptian love songs from around 1300–1100 BCE, which Michael V. Fox studied alongside the Song: their lovers call each other “brother” and “sister”, as here, and share many of its images.

Twentieth-century readers added new questions. Phyllis Trible read the Song as a return to Eden: in Genesis a garden is lost and the woman is told that her desire will be for her husband and he will rule over her (Genesis 3:16); in the Song a garden is regained and the woman says, “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (7:10). Feminist scholars such as Athalya Brenner, J. Cheryl Exum and Carol Meyers have explored the Song’s female voice, its mothers and its brothers, its violence (5:7) and its freedoms. Today the plain reading, a poem about human love, is the starting point for almost every scholar, while many religious readers hold it together with the older allegories, finding in human love a likeness of divine love rather than a rival to it.

intro.title: How the poetry works
p: Hebrew poetry rhymes in thought rather than in sound. Its basic unit is a line in two (sometimes three) parts, where the second part echoes, sharpens or extends the first: “Your eyes are doves behind your veil. / Your hair is like a flock of goats.” Often the second half intensifies: “I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer” (5:6). This parallelism gives the Song its rocking, incantatory rhythm, and it survives translation better than rhyme or metre would.

The Song’s most distinctive form is the descriptive praise song that scholars call a waṣf, after Wetzstein. It moves through the body, usually from head to foot (4:1–7, 6:4–7) or foot to head (7:1–5), comparing each part to something in the world: hair to a flock of goats, teeth to shorn ewes, a neck to a tower, a nose to the tower of Lebanon. Once, unusually, the woman sings one of her lover (5:10–16), and her images are of gold, ivory, jewels and cedar, as if he were a statue in a temple.

These comparisons puzzle modern readers who try to picture them. A woman whose nose is a tower is not an attractive sight. But the images do not work by shape; they work by effect. Goats streaming down a hillside at dusk give the movement and shimmer of dark hair; ewes coming up from the washing, “each one with its twin”, give whiteness, freshness and the satisfaction of nothing missing; a tower hung with shields gives poise, dignity, and the faint sense of something not easily approached. Othmar Keel showed how many of the Song’s images echo the visual art of the ancient Near East, where doves were messengers of love and gazelles belonged to the goddess of love. The question to ask of each image is not “what does it look like?” but “what does it feel like?”

The poem speaks to all five senses. It is full of scents (nard, myrrh, henna, cinnamon, the smell of Lebanon), tastes (wine, honey, milk, raisin cakes, apples, pomegranate juice), sounds (the beloved’s voice, the turtledove, knocking at night), touch (the left hand under the head) and sight. Places are used the same way. En-gedi is an oasis by the Dead Sea; Lebanon means cedars, snow and height; Gilead means wild hill country; Heshbon has pools; Kedar means black tents in the desert; Tirzah and Jerusalem mean beauty and royal splendour. A place name is a colour and a feeling, not a map reference.

Finally, the Song is built on returns. Refrains bind it together: the oath to the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love (2:7, 3:5, 8:4), the embrace (2:6, 8:3), the declaration of mutual belonging (2:16, 6:3, 7:10), the gazelle on the mountains (2:9, 2:17, 8:14), the question “Who is this coming up from the wilderness?” (3:6, 8:5). Scenes repeat with differences, most strikingly the two night searches (3:1–5 and 5:2–8), the first ending in finding, the second in loss and injury. The effect is less like a story than like love itself: the same longings, coming round again, never quite the same.

intro.title: About this translation
p: The English text in this app is an original rendering made for it, from the Hebrew Masoretic text, the standard text of the Hebrew Bible. It aims to be accurate and to read as poetry in plain modern English: keeping the ancient images (gazelles, nard, the tower of David), keeping the repetitions that the Hebrew insists on, and avoiding both archaic language and modern slang. Where the Hebrew is obscure, and in the Song it often is, the translation makes a choice and the commentary explains it and gives the main alternatives.

Verse numbers follow English Bibles. In the Hebrew text, the verse English Bibles number 6:13 (“Return, return, Shulammite”) is 7:1, so chapter 7 in Hebrew runs from 7:1 to 7:14 where English runs from 7:1 to 7:13. Where a verse divides between two speakers, it is split and marked a and b.

A few choices deserve mention here. The word dōdîm, which older versions render “love” and which more precisely means lovemaking or caresses (1:2, 4:10, 7:12), is translated “love”, because English has no single word that is both tender and physical without being clinical or crude; the commentary says more. At 8:6 the Hebrew šalhebetyâ ends in -yâ, which can be a short form of the divine name or simply an intensifier (“a mighty flame”); this translation gives “a very flame of the Lord” to keep both possibilities in view, and the commentary explains why it matters that this may be the only place God is named. “The Lord” stands for the divine name as in most English Bibles.

Everything apart from the words of the poem is editorial: the speaker labels, the division into twenty-five passages, and the passage titles. The divisions follow the poem’s own refrains and changes of scene, and broadly agree with most modern commentaries, but other divisions are possible, and the poem flows from one passage into the next. It is best read straight through at least once.

intro.title: How to use this app
p: Read takes you through the whole Song from beginning to end, with each passage’s title as a signpost; it takes about fifteen minutes. Passages is for study: each of the twenty-five passages has its text, an explanation of what is happening, a few Hebrew words that unlock it, how Jewish and Christian readers have heard it, reflections for your own life, and a question to sit with. Themes follows the Song’s recurring images, such as the garden, the gazelle and the night search, across the whole poem.

Press and hold to select any words, then tap Quote to keep them or Note to write about them: a thought, a question, an answer you find later. Your notebook collects them and leads you back to the passage, and passages you have written about get a small mark in the margin. Everything you save stays on this device.
